2211	    With the development of LLMs, a new category called reasoning LLMs (Treude
2212	and Kula, 2025) has emerged to handle more complex tasks. The distinction
2213	between reasoning and non-reasoning LLMs primarily lies in their approach
2214	to problem-solving and the complexity of tasks they can handle. Reasoning
2215	LLMs can perform step-by-step processing and tackle multi-step tasks like
2216	code-related challenges. For example, DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al, 2025) and
2217	QwQ-plus (Cloud, 2024) use reinforcement learning techniques (e.g., GRPO)
2218	to enhance their reasoning abilities. Non-reasoning LLMs, such as GPT-4o,
2219	generate responses based on learned patterns without explicit intermediate
2220	reasoning steps. To further validate our findings, we selected DeepSeek-R1 and
2221	QwQ-plus as our studied reasoning LLMs to evaluate their effectiveness in
2222	detecting function-level and line-level multilingual vulnerabilities. To ensure
2223	experimental fairness and maximize the capabilities of reasoning LLMs, we
2224	selected the DeepSeek-R1 with 671B parameters and the default QwQ-plus
2225	model, whose parameters are not publicly available. To minimize prompt-
2226	related variability, we used the same zero-shot prompt described in Section 3
2227	for both reasoning and non-reasoning LLMs.

2265	4.4 Data Leakage Analysis
2266	
2267	Given that LLMs are pre-trained on extensive open-source corpora, there is
2268	a substantial risk of data leakage where standard test samples may already
2269	exist in the model’s pre-training data. To mitigate this concern, we employ the
2270	REEF data collection methodology to curate a dataset of recent vulnerabilities
2271	from 2024 to 2025. We maintain experimental consistency by applying the
2272	identical preprocessing pipeline and test split ratio (10%) described in Section
2273	2.1. This yields 3,138 function-level samples (balanced 1:1 between vulnerable
2274	and benign functions) and 1,328 line-level samples. Finally, we evaluate GPT-4,
2275	the best-performing model trained on the original dataset, on these temporally
2276	splitting test sets to assess its ability to generalize to future data. The results
2277	of this evaluation are presented in Table 10.
2278	    For function-level detection, the combination of instruction tuning with
2279	few-shot prompting demonstrates superior generalization capabilities compared
2280	to the zero-shot baseline. Specifically, the few-shot configuration achieves an F1-
2281	score of 0.7804 and an MCC of 0.5767, representing a substantial improvement
2282	over the zero-shot performance (F1-score of 0.4396 and MCC of 0.1056). In the
2283	case of line-level detection, we observe that the model retains discriminative
2284	power on unseen data. The few-shot configuration yields the highest stability
2285	with an F1-score of 0.3450 and an MCC of 0.3301. While the absolute values
2286	are lower than those at the function level, reflecting the inherent difficulty of

2315

2317	compare models fairly, isolate intrinsic discriminative ability, and avoid con-

2319	language models (See Table 10) on an imbalance dataset for establishing a
2320	deployment-faithful stress test that reveals how models behave when class skew

2453	4.6 Deployment Cost of LLMs and PLMs on Multilingual Vulnerability
2454	Detection
2455	
2456	Evaluating deployment cost is critical for assessing the practicality of mul-
2457	tilingual vulnerability detection approaches, as real-world adoption depends
2458	not only on detection accuracy but also on economic feasibility. While several
2459	recent studies on LLM-based vulnerability detection (Du et al, 2024; Lu et al,
2460	2024) have reported promising performance, they often overlook deployment
2461	cost, leaving a gap in understanding the trade-off between accuracy and opera-
2462	tional expenses. In contrast, prior work on software engineering tasks such as
2463	SWE-Bench (Yang et al, 2024b; Yu et al, 2025a) has established reporting API
2464

2466	
2467	42                                                                   W. Dong et al.
2468	
2469	
2470	usage costs as a standard practice for evaluating LLM-based solutions, which
2471	we follow in this study.
2472	    For LLMs with more than 100B parameters, such as GPT-3.5-Turbo and
2473	GPT-4o, deployment typically requires data center–grade GPU infrastructure,
2474	making API-based usage a common and practical choice. As shown in Table 12,
2475	for function-level detection with instruction tuning, the training costs for GPT-
2476	3.5-Turbo and GPT-4o are approximately $27.54 and $86.07, respectively, with
2477	input costs of about $1.32 and $1.65, and output costs of about $0.01 and
2478	$0.03. For line-level detection, the training costs are approximately $19.01 and
2479	$59.42, with input costs of about $0.76 and $0.95, and output costs of about
2480	$0.24 and $0.60.
2481	    In contrast, PLMs such as CodeBERT, UniXcoder, CodeT5, and CodeT5P
2482	typically have fewer than 0.3B parameters, allowing them to be trained and
2483	deployed on consumer-grade GPUs. As such, their deployment costs are lim-
2484	ited to compute resources (e.g., GPU/hour) without incurring per-token API
2485	charges.

753	2.4 Metrics
754	
755	Following existing work (Fu and Tantithamthavorn, 2022; Steenhoek et al,
756	2024a), we adopted four widely-used metrics, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and
757	F1-score, to assess all our studied models’ effectiveness in detecting function-
758	level multilingual vulnerability as a binary classification task. Accuracy mea-
759	sures the proportion of correctly predicted instances out of all instances. Pre-
760	cision quantifies how many of the predicted positive instances are actually
761	correct, while Recall assesses the proportion of actual positive instances cor-
762	rectly predicted by the model. The F1-score combines precision and recall
763	into a single metric, providing a balanced view especially useful when dealing
764	with imbalanced datasets. Specifically, in our study, we used binary-averaged
765	Precision, Recall, and F1-score because function-level vulnerability detection
766	can be formulated as a binary classification task. For line-level multilingual
767	vulnerability detection, we formulated the line-level detection task as a binary
768	classification problem for each code line by following the existing work (Ding
769	et al, 2024b). Therefore, we also adopted Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and
770	F1-score to assess all our studied models’ effectiveness in detecting line-level
771	multilingual vulnerability.
772	    Furthermore, we adopted the False Positive Rate (FPR) to measure how
773	often a classifier incorrectly predicts the positive class when the actual class
774	is negative, and False Negative Rate (FNR) to quantify how often the model
775	mistakenly classifies positive instances as negative. In vulnerability detection,
776	false positives (when clean code is flagged as vulnerable) cause developers to

796	Correlation Coefficient (MCC) and Area Under the Receiver Operating Charac-

798	nerability detection at both the function and line levels. MCC serves as a robust
799	measure of binary classification quality by accounting for all four quadrants

801	of the confusion matrix, calculated as √                                         .

803	Complementing this, AUC is employed to evaluate the model’s discriminative
804	ability across all possible classification thresholds. Statistically, AUC represents
805	the probability that a randomly selected vulnerable instance will be ranked
806	higher than a benign one, making it invariant to the specific choice of threshold.
807	We compute the AUC by using the trapezoidal rule.
808	    To reduce ambiguity in calculating metrics across multiple programming
809	languages, we use Accuracy as an illustrative example. Suppose our test set
810	consists of only two languages: Python and Java. Java contains one sample
811	and Python contains two samples. A model correctly predicts one Java sample
812	and one Python sample. Instead of calculating Accuracy for each language
813	separately (Python: 50%, Java: 100%) and then averaging those percentages
814	(75%), we aggregate all samples first. The Total Correct Predictions is two and
815	the Total Samples is three. The global Accuracy is calculated as Accuracy =
816	 Total Correct Predictions
817	       Total Samples       = 23 ≈ 66.7%. This approach ensures that performance
818	is weighted by the actual distribution of samples in each language, providing
819	an objective measurement of the holistic performance of PLMs and LLMs.

851	3.1 RQ1: How effective are PLMs and LLMs in detecting multilingual
852	vulnerabilities at the function-level?
853	
854	Approach. This research question provides a comparative analysis of perfor-
855	mance between various PLMs and LLMs with different strategies in detecting
856	function-level multilingual vulnerability. Specifically, we investigated the effec-
857	tiveness of eight PLMs and five LLMs. The model details are summarized in
858	Section 2.2. We now detail the training/inference process below.
859	    Regarding PLMs, they are pre-trained on a corpus of natural language and
860	source code snippets from various programming languages, but they have not
861	been exposed to the task of function-level vulnerability detection, particularly
862	across multilingual vulnerability. Prior studies (Fu and Tantithamthavorn, 2022;
863	Steenhoek et al, 2023, 2024a) have demonstrated the effectiveness of fine-tuned
864	PLMs for function-level vulnerability detection. Therefore, we fine-tune all
865	studied open-source PLMs (i.e., CodeBert, CodeT5, CodeT5P, UniXCoder,
866	and LineVul) on the function-level training set. The model architecture for
867	function-level multilingual vulnerability detection employs a hybrid design
868	that integrates a PLM encoder with a specialized binary classification head.
869	Specifically, the binary classifier is implemented as a multi-layer perceptron
870	(MLP) that operates on the aggregate sequence representation. To facilitate
871	non-linear mapping and mitigate overfitting, the architecture incorporates
872	a hyperbolic tangent (tanh) activation function interleaved with stochastic
873	dropout layers. The forward pass begins by extracting the representation of
874	the leading sequence token (equivalent to the [CLS] or <s> token), which is
875	then processed through a dense layer and non-linearities. The final output of
876	this classification head is the raw logit, representing the model’s unnormalized
877	confidence score before being mapped to the binary prediction space. We train
878	all parameters of both the encoder and binary classifier through supervised
879	learning on the function-level training set. The trained encoder outputs a code
880	embedding representing the given input given code. This embedding is then
881	fed into the trained binary classifier, which produces a binomial distribution
882	indicating the probability of the given function being vulnerable. For closed-
883	source PLMs (i.e., Text-Embedding-Ada-002, Text-Embedding-3-Small, and
884	Text-Embedding-3-Large), we follow the same training and inference approach.
885	Since these PLMs do not allow access to their parameters, we treat them as
886	frozen encoders and only train the binary classifier.

1212	3.2 RQ2: How effective are PLMs and LLMs in detecting multilingual
1213	vulnerabilities at the line level?
1214	
1215	Approach. This research question focuses on a comparative analysis of per-
1216	formance between different PLMs and LLMs with various strategies in de-
1217	tecting line-level multilingual vulnerability. Specifically, we investigated the
1218	effectiveness of four PLMs and five LLMs. In this case, we excluded three
1219	Text-Embedding Models and LineVul. The Text-Embedding Models can only
1220	provide a single embedding for a given function, making them unsuitable for
1221	line-level detection. LineVul uses an unsupervised learning approach, which
1222	would be unfair to compare with the supervised learning method used in our
1223	experiment. We detail the training and inference process below.
1224	    Regarding PLMs, we adopt a line-level embedding approach to align with
1225	the task of detecting vulnerabilities at the line-level. Specifically, we represented
1226	each vulnerable function using up to nlines = 113 lines, with each line containing
1227	up to ntokens = 31 tokens. This design is based on the observation that 95% of
1228	functions in our dataset contain fewer than 113 lines. Each input function is
1229	embedded into a tensor of shape (nlines , ntokens , dmodel ), where dmodel = 768 is
1230	the hidden dimension of the embedding. To obtain line-level representations, we
1231	summarized each line by applying a single-layer Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)
1232	over the token dimension (ntokens ), producing a tensor of shape (nlines , dmodel ).
1233	We formulated the task as a multi-label classification problem, aiming to
1234	identify which lines within a vulnerable function are vulnerable. Each vulnerable
1235	function contains at least one, and potentially multiple, vulnerable lines. We
1236	added a classification head for each PLM that outputs a single value per line,
1237	followed by a sigmoid activation function. A line is classified as vulnerable if
1238	its output exceeds a threshold of 0.5.
1239	    Regarding LLMs, we expected to use their in-context learning capabilities
1240	to achieve line-level multilingual vulnerability detection with or without in-
1241	struction tuning. Line-level detection required LLMs to identify vulnerable code

1248	lines, but previous studies (Fu et al, 2023b) and our initial experiments have
1249	shown that LLMs cannot accurately distinguish code lines based on line breaks.
1250	To address this issue, we re-structured the functions by adding tags (i.e., Line
1251	N:) in front of each code line. Without instruction tuning, we used zero-shot
1252	or few-shot prompts to guide LLMs in predicting vulnerable line numbers (i.e.,
1253	tags of lines) and their corresponding code. With instruction tuning, we first
1254	performed supervised fine-tuning on our instruction-filled line-level training
1255	set. We then prompted these instruction-tuned LLMs to generate vulnerable
1256	line numbers and corresponding code using zero-shot or few-shot prompting.
1257	
1258	    To evaluate the effectiveness of the studied PLMs and LLMs in detecting
1259	line-level multilingual vulnerability, we used common classification metrics:
1260	Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, FPR, FNR, MCC, and AUC, as detailed
1261	in 2.4. Since our task involves classifying each line of code within a function, we
1262	faced a challenge with imbalanced data, i.e., most code lines are non-vulnerable,
1263	creating an uneven distribution in our line-level dataset. For this reason, we
1264	chose F1-score as our primary metric.

1459	(0.8644) than GPT-4o (0.8116), indicating that while GPT-4o is more effective
1460	at the current threshold, the PLM may possess broader discriminative potential
1461	across different classification thresholds. Although CodeT5P achieves slightly
1462	higher Recall (0.7673 vs. GPT-4o’s 0.6307), its lower Precision substantially
1463	limits its practical utility, as it generates many more false-positive predictions.
1464	Supporting evidence comes from the FPR and FNR metrics. GPT-4o achieves
1465	a much lower FPR (0.0074 vs. CodeT5P’s 0.0385), though it has a higher FNR
1466	(0.3693 vs. CodeT5P’s 0.2327).

1504	multilingual vulnerability detection?
1505	
1506	Approach. This research question aims to deepen our understanding of the
1507	performance of various PLMs and LLMs with different strategies in detecting
1508	multilingual vulnerability at the function-level and line-level. According to
1509	RQ1 and RQ2, we selected the best-performing PLMs and LLMs with various
1510	strategies as our representative models. In our function-level multilingual
1511	vulnerability detection analysis, we selected models based on Accuracy metric.
1512	We chose CodeT5P for PLMs and evaluated four LLM variants: Llama 3
1513	using zero-shot prompting (ZSP), and three GPT-4o configurations - few-shot
1514	prompting (FSP), instruction tuning with zero-shot prompting (ITZSP), and
1515	instruction tuning with few-shot prompting (ITFSP). For line-level multilingual
1516	vulnerability detection, we based our model selection on F1-score performance.
1517	We maintained CodeT5P as our PLM representative and utilized the four
1518	GPT-4o variants (ZSP, FSP, ITZSP, and ITFSP) for LLM representatives. Our
1519	orthogonality analysis consists of the following three perspectives:
1520	 – The unique correct and incorrect detection. To investigate the com-
1521	   plementarity of PLMs and LLMs, we performed a set-membership analysis
1522	   using Venn diagrams. We categorized the results based on the instance-level
1523	   alignment between model predictions and ground-truth labels. Specifically,
1524	   we constructed sets of Correct Detections (True Positives and True Nega-
1525	   tives) and Incorrect Detections (False Positives and False Negatives) for
1526	   each model. This approach allows us to quantify the orthogonality of the
1527	   models—identifying whether LLMs succeed on the specific code instances
1528	   where PLMs fail, and vice-versa. The Venn diagrams thus represent the
1529	   distribution of unique and shared performance over the total population of

2006	    The structural comparison, summarized in Figure 10, reveals distinct oper-
2007	ational profiles for each model architecture when analyzing median values. The
2008	most significant differentiator between the models is their ability to handle
2009	logical complexity. As evidenced by the Median CC metric, the total median for
2010	samples correctly detected only by the LLM is 4.0, compared to a median CC
2011	of 2.0 for samples detected only by the PLM. This disparity is particularly stark
2012	in languages like C#, where the LLM-exclusive successes had a median CC
2013	of 3.0 while the PLM-exclusive successes reached 5.0. Overall, the lower total
2014	median for the PLM indicates that CodeT5P struggles to maintain coherence
2015	in code characterized by heavy branching, whereas LLM demonstrates superior
2016	reasoning capabilities in tracing complex execution paths.
2017	    A similar trend is evident when analyzing metrics related to code verbosity
2018	and length. The LLM exhibited a clear advantage in processing larger contexts,
2019	with the median for its exclusive correct predictions reaching 135.5 tokens and
2020	19.0 lines of code (LOC). Conversely, the samples where the PLM uniquely
2021	succeeded were notably shorter, with median values of 96.0 tokens and 15.0
2022	LOC. This data suggests that the PLM’s performance degrades as the input
2023	volume increases, likely due to fixed context window constraints or limited
2024	attention capacity. LLM, however, remains more robust in verbose scenarios,
2025	identifying vulnerabilities where the PLM fails due to information overload.
2026	    While the LLM generally dominates in measures of scale and logical com-
2027	plexity, the analysis of Median Nesting Degree offers a nuanced counterpoint.
2028	The total median nesting degree for the PLM-exclusive successes was 3.0,
2029	which is higher than the 2.0 observed for the LLM’s unique successes. This
2030	reversal, notably seen in JavaScript where the PLM handled a median nesting
2031	of 4.0 compared to the LLM’s 2.0, implies that while CodeT5P falters with
2032	broad logical branching, it remains highly effective at capturing local structural
2033	patterns even when they are deeply nested. Regarding interface complexity, the
2034	Median Parameter Count also reflects this trend; the LLM correctly classified
2035	more complex functions in languages like C# (median of 2.0 parameter count
2036	vs 1.0 for PLM), though the total median for both models sat at 2.0.
2037	    The data highlights a trade-off between complexity reasoning and pattern
2038	recognition. The PLM (CodeT5P) falters primarily when faced with higher
2039	logical complexity and extended contexts. In contrast, the LLM (GPT-4o)
2040	occasionally fails on samples that are structurally simpler and shorter but may
2041	contain specific local patterns that the PLM’s training objective captures more
2042	effectively.

2160	    These results indicate that larger LLMs are not the decisive factor in
2161	function-level detection performance. While few-shot prompting works better
2162	with larger models, instruction tuning can lead to under-fitting problems when
2163	there are too many parameters. Consequently, when using a larger model
2164	for function-level detection, careful instruction tuning and appropriate hyper-
2165	parameter (e.g. number of adapters in LoRA) selection are essential. Larger
2166	LLMs have a more significant impact on line-level vulnerability detection,
2167	especially when using Llama 3, likely due to their more concentrated training
2168	sets and more informative labels. The differences between these models, de-
2169	spite having the same parameters, can be attributed to the models’ inherent
2170	characteristics. For example, Llama 3 differs from Code Llama by using a
2171	new tokenizer and training on a larger token dataset, which can significantly
2172	affect the LLMs’ fundamental ability and then further affect the effectiveness
2173	of instruction tuning.

2211	    With the development of LLMs, a new category called reasoning LLMs (Treude
2212	and Kula, 2025) has emerged to handle more complex tasks. The distinction
2213	between reasoning and non-reasoning LLMs primarily lies in their approach
2214	to problem-solving and the complexity of tasks they can handle. Reasoning
2215	LLMs can perform step-by-step processing and tackle multi-step tasks like
2216	code-related challenges. For example, DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al, 2025) and
2217	QwQ-plus (Cloud, 2024) use reinforcement learning techniques (e.g., GRPO)
2218	to enhance their reasoning abilities. Non-reasoning LLMs, such as GPT-4o,
2219	generate responses based on learned patterns without explicit intermediate
2220	reasoning steps. To further validate our findings, we selected DeepSeek-R1 and
2221	QwQ-plus as our studied reasoning LLMs to evaluate their effectiveness in
2222	detecting function-level and line-level multilingual vulnerabilities. To ensure
2223	experimental fairness and maximize the capabilities of reasoning LLMs, we
2224	selected the DeepSeek-R1 with 671B parameters and the default QwQ-plus
2225	model, whose parameters are not publicly available. To minimize prompt-
2226	related variability, we used the same zero-shot prompt described in Section 3
2227	for both reasoning and non-reasoning LLMs.

2265	4.4 Data Leakage Analysis
2266	
2267	Given that LLMs are pre-trained on extensive open-source corpora, there is
2268	a substantial risk of data leakage where standard test samples may already
2269	exist in the model’s pre-training data. To mitigate this concern, we employ the
2270	REEF data collection methodology to curate a dataset of recent vulnerabilities
2271	from 2024 to 2025. We maintain experimental consistency by applying the
2272	identical preprocessing pipeline and test split ratio (10%) described in Section
2273	2.1. This yields 3,138 function-level samples (balanced 1:1 between vulnerable
2274	and benign functions) and 1,328 line-level samples. Finally, we evaluate GPT-4,
2275	the best-performing model trained on the original dataset, on these temporally
2276	splitting test sets to assess its ability to generalize to future data. The results
2277	of this evaluation are presented in Table 10.
2278	    For function-level detection, the combination of instruction tuning with
2279	few-shot prompting demonstrates superior generalization capabilities compared
2280	to the zero-shot baseline. Specifically, the few-shot configuration achieves an F1-
2281	score of 0.7804 and an MCC of 0.5767, representing a substantial improvement
2282	over the zero-shot performance (F1-score of 0.4396 and MCC of 0.1056). In the
2283	case of line-level detection, we observe that the model retains discriminative
2284	power on unseen data. The few-shot configuration yields the highest stability

2532	5 Threats to Validity
2533	
2534	External Threats primarily stem from our choice of multilingual vulnerability
2535	dataset and automated vulnerability detection approaches. Our study focused
2536	on the REEF dataset covering seven programming languages, which may limit
2537	the generalizability of our findings to other languages. To address this limitation,
2538	we plan to expand our vulnerability collection to include more programming
2539	languages and timelines using the REEF collection framework. To minimize
2540	methodological threats, we performed a comprehensive literature review to
2541	ensure our selected PLMs and LLMs for automated vulnerability detection
2542	represent current state-of-the-art solutions.
2543	    Internal Threat relates to our implementation and utilization of the studied
2544	approaches. To address this, we carefully implemented all existing approaches
2545	following their original replication packages, with two authors conducting
2546	thorough code reviews. For PLMs, we followed the hyperparameter settings
2547	recommended by the original authors to ensure a fair reproduction of their
2548	approaches. However, the 512-token input limit of the smaller PLMs we used,
2549	which cannot be extended during fine-tuning, may restrict the models’ ability

2549	which cannot be extended during fine-tuning, may restrict the models’ ability
2550	to capture context in longer code snippets. We acknowledge this architectural
2551	constraint as a limitation of our experimental setup. For LLMs, we utilized
2552	official channels, accessing public models (DeepSeek-Coder, Code Llama, and
2553	Llama3) via HuggingFace and invoking APIs (GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4o)
2554	according to documented guidelines. Besides, this study excludes certain state-
2555	of-the-art LLMs fine-tuned for vulnerability detection, as many target single
2556	languages (mainly C/C++) or lack line-level localization. Since our focus is
2557	multilingual and dual-granularity performance, these models fall outside our
2558	scope. While this limits comparison with customized tools, our evaluation of 11
2559	diverse models with multiple stretagies, from CodeBERT to GPT-4o, provides

2561	as a line-level baseline and will prioritize specialized models as they support
2562	broader languages in future studies.

2716	focuses on function-level classification, we provide a dual-granularity analysis
2717	that includes line-level localization, offering a more fine-grained perspective on
2718	model interpretability. Finally, we explore a broader array of prompting and
2719	tuning strategies specifically tailored for the multilingual scenario, providing
2720	a comprehensive assessment of how these models generalize beyond single-
2721	language constraints. In the multilingual settings, Cao et al (2022) propose
2722	a framework based on model distillation and pre-trained language models
2723	(i.e., CodeBERT) for multilingual vulnerability detection. However, their work
2724	focuses solely on function-level detection. In contrast, our study is a compre-

2728	Large Language Models for Multilingual Vulnerability Detection                  47
2729	
2730	
2731	hensive empirical study by examining dual-granularity detection across 6 PLMs
2732	and 5 LLMs, employing different prompting strategies, zero-shot, few-shot,
2733	and instruction-tuning, on seven programming languages. We also incorporate
2734	line-level localization to provide finer-grained security insights.
2735	     Notably, researchers have observed significant variations in the detection
2736	difficulty of different vulnerability types. Studies by Russell et al (2018), Zou
2737	et al (2021), and Xu et al (2022) indicate that detecting certain types of
2738	vulnerabilities is more challenging. Furthermore, Hin et al (2022) evaluated
2739	model performance in cross-project settings using a leave-one-out approach and
2740	found a slight decline in performance under such scenarios. However, as modern
2741	software development increasingly trends toward multilingual integration, the
2742	diversity of codebases introduces new challenges for software security. The
2743	effectiveness of existing vulnerability detection methods in multilingual scenar-
2744	ios remains unverified, making it difficult to meet the demands of real-world
2745	development.
2746	
2747	
2748	
2749	
2750	7 Conclusions
2751	
2752	This work systematically evaluated the performance of pre-trained language
2753	models (PLMs) and large language models (LLMs) across seven programming
2754	languages for multilingual vulnerability detection at both function and line
2755	granularity. Our findings highlight that LLMs, particularly GPT-4o enhanced
2756	with instruction tuning and few-shot prompting, significantly outperform ex-
2757	isting PLMs like CodeT5P. Specifically, GPT-4o achieved superior accuracy
2758	in function-level detection and markedly higher precision and F1-scores in
2759	line-level detection tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and versatility in mul-
2760	tilingual contexts. Additionally, orthogonality analysis revealed that GPT-4o
2761	not only detects vulnerabilities uniquely missed by other models but also excels
2762	in identifying high-severity vulnerabilities, emphasizing its practical value in
2763	real-world security applications. Despite these promising results, our study
2764	also reveals that the size and reasoning capabilities of LLMs do not necessarily
2765	correlate directly with improved vulnerability detection performance.
2766	    Meanwhile, our study opens up several potential future research directions,
2767	including: extending the scale of multilingual vulnerability benchmark, introduc-
2768	ing different intermediate representations for unifying the code representation,
2769	and refining the PLM/LLM learning strategies. For instance, beyond super-
2770	vised fine-tuning and instruction tuning, strategies like multi-task learning or
2771	meta-learning could better align PLMs and LLMs with multilingual domains by
2772	reducing the performance gap between high-resource and low-resource program-
2773	ming languages. In general, our work provides critical insight and foundational
2774	knowledge that can guide the advancement of robust multilingual vulnerability
2775	detection tools, addressing key limitations identified in existing approaches.

# SecVulEval: Context-Aware Benchmarking of LLMs for Vulnerability Detection

- Authors: Ahmed, Md Basim Uddin; Harzevili, Nima Shiri; Shin, Jiho; Pham, Hung Viet; Wang, Song
- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 3rd ACM International Conference on AI-Powered Software (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3805760.3814932 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3805760.3814932
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

> Version note: the text analysed is the arXiv preprint 2505.19828v1 (26 May 2025), titled "SecVulEval: Benchmarking LLMs for Real-World C/C++ Vulnerability Detection", marked "Preprint. Under review." (p. 1). The published AIware 2026 version may differ in title, numbers and content. See Analyst notes.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Build a C/C++ vulnerability benchmark with statement-level labels, rich metadata and program context (function arguments, external functions, type declarations, globals, execution environment), and use it to test how well current LLMs detect and localise real vulnerabilities (p. 1, p. 2).
- [A] Motivation: existing datasets (BigVul, CVEFixes, DiverseVul, PrimeVul, MegaVul, etc.) are function-level only, lack context, contain duplicates/mislabels, and line-level labels (BigVul, CVEFixes, SVEN) are line fragments rather than statements (p. 2, p. 3).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- No formal RQs or hypotheses. Two experiments: (1) LLM vulnerability detection at function and statement level; (2) LLM identification of the context needed for detection (p. 6, p. 7).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: benchmark construction from NVD + GitHub commits, followed by an empirical evaluation of 5 LLMs inside a multi-agent pipeline, with manual judging of statement-level outputs (p. 4-p. 8).
- Approach / model / intervention: five-agent pipeline: Normalization Agent (tree-sitter AST, no LLM), Planning Agent (function summary + checklist of up to 8 "red-flag" cues), Context Agent (asks for up to 6 external symbols per round, max 3 rounds; definitions fetched with tree-sitter), Detection Agent (verdict + vulnerable statements + reason), Validation Agent (agrees or disagrees; Detection reruns up to 3 times) (p. 7, p. 14-p. 16). [A] Authors claim it is the first LLM multi-agent pipeline applied to vulnerability detection (p. 7).
- Models: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, Deepseek-Coder-33B-Instruct, Codestral-22B-v0.1 (open weights, HuggingFace), GPT-4.1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet (p. 8).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: none beyond the 5 LLMs. No static-analysis tool, no fine-tuned DL/PLM detector, no single-LLM (non-agent) baseline, and no with/without-context ablation for detection (not reported).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): NVD CVEs (non-REJECTED) for products previously identified as C/C++ in BigVul, CVEFixes and PrimeVul, plus NVD keyword search ("C++", "C language", ".cpp"); only CVEs with an NVD "Patch" reference to a commit in the original (non-forked) repository; commit data via GitHub REST API (p. 4).
- Filtering: non-C/C++ files removed; only single-commit fixes kept (43 multi-commit CVEs dropped); files with no function changes removed; tangled changes filtered by keeping only functions solely modified in a file or named in the CVE/commit message; de-duplication by md5 of whitespace-normalised function text (p. 5).
- Sample size (N) and unit: 25,440 functions = 10,998 vulnerable + 14,442 non-vulnerable; 5,867 CVEs, 707 projects, 145 CWEs, CVEs from 1999-2024 (p. 6, p. 9). Function size 4-541 lines (2.5-97.5 percentile), median 44 lines; on average about 4 statements deleted and 6 added per function (p. 6). Linux alone contributes 1,920 CVEs and 2,793 vulnerable functions (p. 5).
- Non-vulnerable functions: their exact definition (fixed versions of vulnerable functions vs. other unchanged functions) is not explicitly stated; the text says both "vulnerable version" and "fixed version" copies are kept for each changed function (p. 5). Not reported precisely.
- Context labels: generated automatically by GPT-4.1 from CWE, function body, patch, commit message and CVE description; manual check of 100 random samples (4 excluded as N/A) gave 82.98 ± 9.68% accuracy (99% CI) (p. 6).
- Detection experiment sample: 300 functions randomly selected from the Top-25 CWE types, manually validated; 120 of them vulnerable (p. 8, p. 12, p. 13).
- Data availability: dataset on HuggingFace (arag0rn/SecVulEval) and code on GitHub (basimbd/SecVulEval) (p. 3); "friendly license" for research and commercial use (p. 12).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings: pass@1, temperature 0.1; Intel Xeon Gold 6442Y CPU, 4 x NVIDIA L40S GPUs, 250 GiB RAM; open models via transformers.pipeline (p. 8, p. 17). Prompts for all four LLM agents given verbatim; prompts were rewritten to stress "*defensive*" research after models refused (p. 13-p. 16). Function and AST inputs may be truncated if too long (p. 14); truncation limit not reported.
- Statement-level TP rules (manual): exact vulnerable statements with correct reasoning; or at least one of several fix locations; or correct statements plus at most two unrelated ones; or only the sink statement / sink + source with correct reasoning (p. 8). Function-level is judged automatically from the `is_vulnerable` field (p. 8).
- Number and independence of manual raters, and inter-rater agreement: not reported.
- Cost/time: open models take 4.97-7.99 minutes per function in total (Codestral 4.97, Qwen 6.03, Deepseek 7.99) (p. 17). Proprietary model time and API cost not reported (p. 17).
- Code availability: GitHub repository (p. 3).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Precision, recall, F1 at function level (is the function vulnerable?) and statement level (are the vulnerable statements identified with correct reasoning?) (p. 7). A function-level TP with wrong reasoning is defined as a statement-level FN (p. 7).
- Context identification: accuracy per context type versus dataset ground truth (which itself is GPT-4.1-generated) (p. 7, p. 9).
- Statistical testing: one-sided Mann-Whitney U tests for function length of detected vs. missed vulnerable functions (p. 12, p. 13). No confidence intervals or significance tests on the detection metrics; single run per model (not reported otherwise).

## 7. Key findings
1. Statement-level detection is poor for all models: F1 = Claude-3.7-Sonnet 23.83%, GPT-4.1 22.38%, Codestral-22B 15.31%, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B 13.57%, Deepseek-Coder-33B 7.14% — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
2. Function-level F1: Claude 53.89%, GPT-4.1 52.25%, Codestral 46.61%, Deepseek 45.71%, Qwen 35.20%; function-level precision is only 35.48-47.41% for every model — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
3. Proprietary models are more "aggressive": function-level recall 75.63% (Claude) and 73.11% (GPT-4.1) but precision 41.86% and 40.65%, lower than Codestral (47.41%) and Deepseek (45.16%); of 300 samples (120 vulnerable) GPT-4.1 and Claude flagged 214 and 215 as vulnerable vs. 116-124 for the open models — [V] (p. 8, p. 13).
4. Statement-level precision is 5.65-15.35% for all models, i.e. most flagged statements/reasons are wrong — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
5. Detected vulnerable functions are much shorter than missed ones: median 14-33 LoC detected vs. 64-71 LoC missed; one-sided Mann-Whitney U p = 0.000197-0.0168 for all five models — [V] (p. 12, p. 13, Table 5).
6. Over-detection concentrates on CWE-476 (NULL dereference, flagged even when an explicit null check exists), CWE-416 (any `free()`/`kfree()` treated as use-after-free) and CWE-190 (arithmetic flagged as overflow without analysis), especially for GPT-4.1 and Claude — [A] qualitative, from manual validation, no counts given (p. 13).
7. LLMs identify needed context poorly: best per type is Claude (external functions 37.00%, type definitions 41.33%, globals 34.53%); function-argument accuracy 0-5.31% for all models; no model identified any environment-level context (1.5% of all contexts) — [V] (p. 9, Table 4).
8. GPT-4.1 identifies required context with 82.98 ± 9.68% accuracy when given the patch, CVE and commit message (dataset-construction setting, not detection) — [V] (p. 6).
9. SecVulEval has 0.0% duplicates vs. 18.9% (CVEFixes), 12.7% (BigVul), 3.3% (DiverseVul) as reported by PrimeVul — [V] for SecVulEval figure; others cited from [5] (p. 3, Table 1).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Context labels were produced by an LLM; manual validation on only 100 samples; "relevant context" is subjective; repository-wide / transitive context not covered (p. 12).
- [A] Manual statement-level judging is subjective and labour-intensive, which limits scale (p. 12).
- [A] Only the largest runnable size of each model was evaluated; conclusions may not hold for smaller sizes (p. 12).
- [A] Multi-commit fixes were excluded for simplicity (p. 5).
- [A] Dataset could be misused to train exploit-seeking models (p. 12).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] No non-LLM baseline at all (no SAST tool, no fine-tuned DL/PLM model, no single-prompt LLM). The paper therefore cannot say whether the multi-agent design helps or hurts, nor how LLMs compare with traditional tools. Based on §3/§5 above (p. 7, p. 8).
- [I] The statement-level recall in Table 3 appears not to follow the stated definition. Reconstructing integer counts from Table 3 and the flag counts on p. 13 (e.g. Claude: 215 flagged, 90 function-level TP, 119 positives, 33 statement-level TP) reproduces every reported statement-level recall exactly as TP_stat / (TP_stat + function-level FN). This means "right function, wrong reasoning" cases were not counted as FN, contrary to the definition on p. 7. Under the stated definition Claude's statement-level recall would be about 27.7% (33/119), not 53.23%, and F1 about 19.8%, not 23.83%. Same pattern for all five models (GPT-4.1 ≈ 26.1% vs. 49.21%). This is our arithmetic on the paper's tables (p. 8, p. 13). It makes the headline numbers optimistic, not pessimistic.
- [I] The implied number of vulnerable functions differs by model (119-126) although the paper says 120 of 300 are vulnerable (p. 13). This suggests unreported exclusions (e.g. failed outputs) per model. Same reconstruction as above.
- [I] The detection evaluation uses only 300 functions (about 1.2% of the benchmark), drawn from Top-25 CWEs only, with no uncertainty reported. Differences of a few points between models (e.g. Claude vs. GPT-4.1, 23.83% vs. 22.38%) are within likely sampling noise (p. 8).
- [I] Circularity in Experiment 2: the "ground truth" context was generated by GPT-4.1 (p. 6), and GPT-4.1 is also one of the evaluated models (p. 9). This makes the context accuracies hard to interpret.
- [I] Task setup differs from SAST use: the pipeline gets one function plus LLM-requested definitions, not the whole repository or build. Results describe LLM function-level review, not project-scale scanning.
- [I] Class balance in the 300-sample set (40% vulnerable) is far from real codebases, so the reported precision would likely drop further in deployment. This rests on the 120/300 count (p. 13).
- [I] Data contamination is not discussed: CVEs up to 2024 and public fixes may be in the training data of all five models (no time-split analysis).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal: manual judging rules are lenient (sink-only counts as TP; up to two extra statements allowed) (p. 8); rater count and agreement not reported; the recall computation inconsistency (§9). Label noise is reduced by heuristics but not measured for the vulnerability labels themselves; only the context labels were validated (p. 5, p. 6).
- External: C/C++ only; Linux is a large share (2,793 of 10,998 vulnerable functions) (p. 5); evaluation limited to Top-25 CWEs and 300 samples (p. 8); five specific LLM versions at temperature 0.1 (p. 8).
- Construct: "correct reasoning" is a human judgement with no stated protocol beyond the four rules (p. 8); function-level detection judged without considering whether the stated reason is right (p. 7, p. 8).
- Statistical conclusion: single run per model, no confidence intervals or tests on Table 3; Mann-Whitney tests are run across five models without multiple-comparison correction (all p < 0.017, so likely robust) (p. 13).
- Reproducibility: dataset, code and full prompts released (p. 3, p. 14-p. 16); hardware and temperature reported (p. 8, p. 17); manual labels for the 300 samples availability not stated.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: use the statement-level and context labels to train and evaluate detection models (p. 10); explore smaller model sizes (p. 12); "advancing statement-level detection is essential" (p. 9).
- Suggested by us [I]: run SAST tools (e.g. CodeQL, Cppcheck) and fine-tuned DL detectors on the same 300-sample subset; report statement-level recall under the stated definition with confidence intervals; ablate the multi-agent pipeline vs. single prompt and with vs. without context; time-split by CVE date to check contamination.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (benchmark quality, granularity, duplication), RQ4 (C/C++, CWE-specific over-detection, function length), RQ5 (context, localisation, false positives), indirectly RQ3 (agentic LLM pipeline with AST/tree-sitter context; execution time) and RQ1 (LLM-only absolute effectiveness, no head-to-head).
- How it informs our work [I]: strong evidence that function-level LLM scores overstate real capability; when correct root cause is required, F1 drops by more than half. Useful for the "evaluation realism" argument and for CWE-level weakness (CWE-476/416/190 false alarms). It cannot answer RQ1 directly because there is no SAST or DL comparison.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | Best LLM (Claude-3.7-Sonnet, multi-agent) reaches 23.83% statement-level F1 and 53.89% function-level F1 on real C/C++ CVEs; function-level precision ≤47.41% for all 5 LLMs | p. 8 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Requiring correct vulnerable statements + reasoning cuts F1 by more than half vs. function-level labels (e.g. GPT-4.1 52.25% → 22.38%) | p. 8 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | SecVulEval: 25,440 de-duplicated C/C++ functions, 5,867 CVEs, 145 CWEs, statement-level + context labels; prior datasets have up to 18.9% duplicates | p. 3, p. 6 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Statement-level recall appears computed without counting wrong-reasoning cases as FN; under the stated definition Claude's recall would be ~27.7%, not 53.23% | p. 7, p. 8, p. 13 | I | moderate |
| RQ4 | All 5 LLMs detect short functions and miss long ones (median 14-33 vs. 64-71 LoC; Mann-Whitney p ≤ 0.0168) | p. 13 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | GPT-4.1 and Claude over-flag CWE-476, CWE-416 and CWE-190 (e.g. null deref despite explicit null check) | p. 13 | A | weak |

# SecVulEval: Context-Aware Benchmarking of LLMs for Vulnerability Detection

- Authors: Ahmed, Md Basim Uddin; Harzevili, Nima Shiri; Shin, Jiho; Pham, Hung Viet; Wang, Song
- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 3rd ACM International Conference on AI-Powered Software (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3805760.3814932 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3805760.3814932
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

> Version note: the text analysed is the arXiv preprint 2505.19828v1 (26 May 2025), titled "SecVulEval: Benchmarking LLMs for Real-World C/C++ Vulnerability Detection", marked "Preprint. Under review." (p. 1). The published AIware 2026 version may differ in title, numbers and content. See Analyst notes.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Build a C/C++ vulnerability benchmark with statement-level labels, rich metadata and program context (function arguments, external functions, type declarations, globals, execution environment), and use it to test how well current LLMs detect and localise real vulnerabilities (p. 1, p. 2).
- [A] Motivation: existing datasets (BigVul, CVEFixes, DiverseVul, PrimeVul, MegaVul, etc.) are function-level only, lack context, contain duplicates/mislabels, and line-level labels (BigVul, CVEFixes, SVEN) are line fragments rather than statements (p. 2, p. 3).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- No formal RQs or hypotheses. Two experiments: (1) LLM vulnerability detection at function and statement level; (2) LLM identification of the context needed for detection (p. 6, p. 7).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: benchmark construction from NVD + GitHub commits, followed by an empirical evaluation of 5 LLMs inside a multi-agent pipeline, with manual judging of statement-level outputs (p. 4-p. 8).
- Approach / model / intervention: five-agent pipeline: Normalization Agent (tree-sitter AST, no LLM), Planning Agent (function summary + checklist of up to 8 "red-flag" cues), Context Agent (asks for up to 6 external symbols per round, max 3 rounds; definitions fetched with tree-sitter), Detection Agent (verdict + vulnerable statements + reason), Validation Agent (agrees or disagrees; Detection reruns up to 3 times) (p. 7, p. 14-p. 16). [A] Authors claim it is the first LLM multi-agent pipeline applied to vulnerability detection (p. 7).
- Models: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, Deepseek-Coder-33B-Instruct, Codestral-22B-v0.1 (open weights, HuggingFace), GPT-4.1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet (p. 8).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: none beyond the 5 LLMs. No static-analysis tool, no fine-tuned DL/PLM detector, no single-LLM (non-agent) baseline, and no with/without-context ablation for detection (not reported).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): NVD CVEs (non-REJECTED) for products previously identified as C/C++ in BigVul, CVEFixes and PrimeVul, plus NVD keyword search ("C++", "C language", ".cpp"); only CVEs with an NVD "Patch" reference to a commit in the original (non-forked) repository; commit data via GitHub REST API (p. 4).
- Filtering: non-C/C++ files removed; only single-commit fixes kept (43 multi-commit CVEs dropped); files with no function changes removed; tangled changes filtered by keeping only functions solely modified in a file or named in the CVE/commit message; de-duplication by md5 of whitespace-normalised function text (p. 5).
- Sample size (N) and unit: 25,440 functions = 10,998 vulnerable + 14,442 non-vulnerable; 5,867 CVEs, 707 projects, 145 CWEs, CVEs from 1999-2024 (p. 6, p. 9). Function size 4-541 lines (2.5-97.5 percentile), median 44 lines; on average about 4 statements deleted and 6 added per function (p. 6). Linux alone contributes 1,920 CVEs and 2,793 vulnerable functions (p. 5).
- Non-vulnerable functions: their exact definition (fixed versions of vulnerable functions vs. other unchanged functions) is not explicitly stated; the text says both "vulnerable version" and "fixed version" copies are kept for each changed function (p. 5). Not reported precisely.
- Context labels: generated automatically by GPT-4.1 from CWE, function body, patch, commit message and CVE description; manual check of 100 random samples (4 excluded as N/A) gave 82.98 ± 9.68% accuracy (99% CI) (p. 6).
- Detection experiment sample: 300 functions randomly selected from the Top-25 CWE types, manually validated; 120 of them vulnerable (p. 8, p. 12, p. 13).
- Data availability: dataset on HuggingFace (arag0rn/SecVulEval) and code on GitHub (basimbd/SecVulEval) (p. 3); "friendly license" for research and commercial use (p. 12).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings: pass@1, temperature 0.1; Intel Xeon Gold 6442Y CPU, 4 x NVIDIA L40S GPUs, 250 GiB RAM; open models via transformers.pipeline (p. 8, p. 17). Prompts for all four LLM agents given verbatim; prompts were rewritten to stress "*defensive*" research after models refused (p. 13-p. 16). Function and AST inputs may be truncated if too long (p. 14); truncation limit not reported.
- Statement-level TP rules (manual): exact vulnerable statements with correct reasoning; or at least one of several fix locations; or correct statements plus at most two unrelated ones; or only the sink statement / sink + source with correct reasoning (p. 8). Function-level is judged automatically from the `is_vulnerable` field (p. 8).
- Number and independence of manual raters, and inter-rater agreement: not reported.
- Cost/time: open models take 4.97-7.99 minutes per function in total (Codestral 4.97, Qwen 6.03, Deepseek 7.99) (p. 17). Proprietary model time and API cost not reported (p. 17).
- Code availability: GitHub repository (p. 3).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Precision, recall, F1 at function level (is the function vulnerable?) and statement level (are the vulnerable statements identified with correct reasoning?) (p. 7). A function-level TP with wrong reasoning is defined as a statement-level FN (p. 7).
- Context identification: accuracy per context type versus dataset ground truth (which itself is GPT-4.1-generated) (p. 7, p. 9).
- Statistical testing: one-sided Mann-Whitney U tests for function length of detected vs. missed vulnerable functions (p. 12, p. 13). No confidence intervals or significance tests on the detection metrics; single run per model (not reported otherwise).

## 7. Key findings
1. Statement-level detection is poor for all models: F1 = Claude-3.7-Sonnet 23.83%, GPT-4.1 22.38%, Codestral-22B 15.31%, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B 13.57%, Deepseek-Coder-33B 7.14% — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
2. Function-level F1: Claude 53.89%, GPT-4.1 52.25%, Codestral 46.61%, Deepseek 45.71%, Qwen 35.20%; function-level precision is only 35.48-47.41% for every model — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
3. Proprietary models are more "aggressive": function-level recall 75.63% (Claude) and 73.11% (GPT-4.1) but precision 41.86% and 40.65%, lower than Codestral (47.41%) and Deepseek (45.16%); of 300 samples (120 vulnerable) GPT-4.1 and Claude flagged 214 and 215 as vulnerable vs. 116-124 for the open models — [V] (p. 8, p. 13).
4. Statement-level precision is 5.65-15.35% for all models, i.e. most flagged statements/reasons are wrong — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
5. Detected vulnerable functions are much shorter than missed ones: median 14-33 LoC detected vs. 64-71 LoC missed; one-sided Mann-Whitney U p = 0.000197-0.0168 for all five models — [V] (p. 12, p. 13, Table 5).
6. Over-detection concentrates on CWE-476 (NULL dereference, flagged even when an explicit null check exists), CWE-416 (any `free()`/`kfree()` treated as use-after-free) and CWE-190 (arithmetic flagged as overflow without analysis), especially for GPT-4.1 and Claude — [A] qualitative, from manual validation, no counts given (p. 13).
7. LLMs identify needed context poorly: best per type is Claude (external functions 37.00%, type definitions 41.33%, globals 34.53%); function-argument accuracy 0-5.31% for all models; no model identified any environment-level context (1.5% of all contexts) — [V] (p. 9, Table 4).
8. GPT-4.1 identifies required context with 82.98 ± 9.68% accuracy when given the patch, CVE and commit message (dataset-construction setting, not detection) — [V] (p. 6).
9. SecVulEval has 0.0% duplicates vs. 18.9% (CVEFixes), 12.7% (BigVul), 3.3% (DiverseVul) as reported by PrimeVul — [V] for SecVulEval figure; others cited from [5] (p. 3, Table 1).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Context labels were produced by an LLM; manual validation on only 100 samples; "relevant context" is subjective; repository-wide / transitive context not covered (p. 12).
- [A] Manual statement-level judging is subjective and labour-intensive, which limits scale (p. 12).
- [A] Only the largest runnable size of each model was evaluated; conclusions may not hold for smaller sizes (p. 12).
- [A] Multi-commit fixes were excluded for simplicity (p. 5).
- [A] Dataset could be misused to train exploit-seeking models (p. 12).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] No non-LLM baseline at all (no SAST tool, no fine-tuned DL/PLM model, no single-prompt LLM). The paper therefore cannot say whether the multi-agent design helps or hurts, nor how LLMs compare with traditional tools. Based on §3/§5 above (p. 7, p. 8).
- [I] The statement-level recall in Table 3 appears not to follow the stated definition. Reconstructing integer counts from Table 3 and the flag counts on p. 13 (e.g. Claude: 215 flagged, 90 function-level TP, 119 positives, 33 statement-level TP) reproduces every reported statement-level recall exactly as TP_stat / (TP_stat + function-level FN). This means "right function, wrong reasoning" cases were not counted as FN, contrary to the definition on p. 7. Under the stated definition Claude's statement-level recall would be about 27.7% (33/119), not 53.23%, and F1 about 19.8%, not 23.83%. Same pattern for all five models (GPT-4.1 ≈ 26.1% vs. 49.21%). This is our arithmetic on the paper's tables (p. 8, p. 13). It makes the headline numbers optimistic, not pessimistic.
- [I] The implied number of vulnerable functions differs by model (119-126) although the paper says 120 of 300 are vulnerable (p. 13). This suggests unreported exclusions (e.g. failed outputs) per model. Same reconstruction as above.
- [I] The detection evaluation uses only 300 functions (about 1.2% of the benchmark), drawn from Top-25 CWEs only, with no uncertainty reported. Differences of a few points between models (e.g. Claude vs. GPT-4.1, 23.83% vs. 22.38%) are within likely sampling noise (p. 8).
- [I] Circularity in Experiment 2: the "ground truth" context was generated by GPT-4.1 (p. 6), and GPT-4.1 is also one of the evaluated models (p. 9). This makes the context accuracies hard to interpret.
- [I] Task setup differs from SAST use: the pipeline gets one function plus LLM-requested definitions, not the whole repository or build. Results describe LLM function-level review, not project-scale scanning.
- [I] Class balance in the 300-sample set (40% vulnerable) is far from real codebases, so the reported precision would likely drop further in deployment. This rests on the 120/300 count (p. 13).
- [I] Data contamination is not discussed: CVEs up to 2024 and public fixes may be in the training data of all five models (no time-split analysis).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal: manual judging rules are lenient (sink-only counts as TP; up to two extra statements allowed) (p. 8); rater count and agreement not reported; the recall computation inconsistency (§9). Label noise is reduced by heuristics but not measured for the vulnerability labels themselves; only the context labels were validated (p. 5, p. 6).
- External: C/C++ only; Linux is a large share (2,793 of 10,998 vulnerable functions) (p. 5); evaluation limited to Top-25 CWEs and 300 samples (p. 8); five specific LLM versions at temperature 0.1 (p. 8).
- Construct: "correct reasoning" is a human judgement with no stated protocol beyond the four rules (p. 8); function-level detection judged without considering whether the stated reason is right (p. 7, p. 8).
- Statistical conclusion: single run per model, no confidence intervals or tests on Table 3; Mann-Whitney tests are run across five models without multiple-comparison correction (all p < 0.017, so likely robust) (p. 13).
- Reproducibility: dataset, code and full prompts released (p. 3, p. 14-p. 16); hardware and temperature reported (p. 8, p. 17); manual labels for the 300 samples availability not stated.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: use the statement-level and context labels to train and evaluate detection models (p. 10); explore smaller model sizes (p. 12); "advancing statement-level detection is essential" (p. 9).
- Suggested by us [I]: run SAST tools (e.g. CodeQL, Cppcheck) and fine-tuned DL detectors on the same 300-sample subset; report statement-level recall under the stated definition with confidence intervals; ablate the multi-agent pipeline vs. single prompt and with vs. without context; time-split by CVE date to check contamination.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (benchmark quality, granularity, duplication), RQ4 (C/C++, CWE-specific over-detection, function length), RQ5 (context, localisation, false positives), indirectly RQ3 (agentic LLM pipeline with AST/tree-sitter context; execution time) and RQ1 (LLM-only absolute effectiveness, no head-to-head).
- How it informs our work [I]: strong evidence that function-level LLM scores overstate real capability; when correct root cause is required, F1 drops by more than half. Useful for the "evaluation realism" argument and for CWE-level weakness (CWE-476/416/190 false alarms). It cannot answer RQ1 directly because there is no SAST or DL comparison.

- Code availability: GitHub repository (p. 3).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Precision, recall, F1 at function level (is the function vulnerable?) and statement level (are the vulnerable statements identified with correct reasoning?) (p. 7). A function-level TP with wrong reasoning is defined as a statement-level FN (p. 7).
- Context identification: accuracy per context type versus dataset ground truth (which itself is GPT-4.1-generated) (p. 7, p. 9).
- Statistical testing: one-sided Mann-Whitney U tests for function length of detected vs. missed vulnerable functions (p. 12, p. 13). No confidence intervals or significance tests on the detection metrics; single run per model (not reported otherwise).

## 7. Key findings
1. Statement-level detection is poor for all models: F1 = Claude-3.7-Sonnet 23.83%, GPT-4.1 22.38%, Codestral-22B 15.31%, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B 13.57%, Deepseek-Coder-33B 7.14% — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
2. Function-level F1: Claude 53.89%, GPT-4.1 52.25%, Codestral 46.61%, Deepseek 45.71%, Qwen 35.20%; function-level precision is only 35.48-47.41% for every model — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
3. Proprietary models are more "aggressive": function-level recall 75.63% (Claude) and 73.11% (GPT-4.1) but precision 41.86% and 40.65%, lower than Codestral (47.41%) and Deepseek (45.16%); of 300 samples (120 vulnerable) GPT-4.1 and Claude flagged 214 and 215 as vulnerable vs. 116-124 for the open models — [V] (p. 8, p. 13).
4. Statement-level precision is 5.65-15.35% for all models, i.e. most flagged statements/reasons are wrong — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
5. Detected vulnerable functions are much shorter than missed ones: median 14-33 LoC detected vs. 64-71 LoC missed; one-sided Mann-Whitney U p = 0.000197-0.0168 for all five models — [V] (p. 12, p. 13, Table 5).
6. Over-detection concentrates on CWE-476 (NULL dereference, flagged even when an explicit null check exists), CWE-416 (any `free()`/`kfree()` treated as use-after-free) and CWE-190 (arithmetic flagged as overflow without analysis), especially for GPT-4.1 and Claude — [A] qualitative, from manual validation, no counts given (p. 13).
7. LLMs identify needed context poorly: best per type is Claude (external functions 37.00%, type definitions 41.33%, globals 34.53%); function-argument accuracy 0-5.31% for all models; no model identified any environment-level context (1.5% of all contexts) — [V] (p. 9, Table 4).
8. GPT-4.1 identifies required context with 82.98 ± 9.68% accuracy when given the patch, CVE and commit message (dataset-construction setting, not detection) — [V] (p. 6).
9. SecVulEval has 0.0% duplicates vs. 18.9% (CVEFixes), 12.7% (BigVul), 3.3% (DiverseVul) as reported by PrimeVul — [V] for SecVulEval figure; others cited from [5] (p. 3, Table 1).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Context labels were produced by an LLM; manual validation on only 100 samples; "relevant context" is subjective; repository-wide / transitive context not covered (p. 12).
- [A] Manual statement-level judging is subjective and labour-intensive, which limits scale (p. 12).
- [A] Only the largest runnable size of each model was evaluated; conclusions may not hold for smaller sizes (p. 12).
- [A] Multi-commit fixes were excluded for simplicity (p. 5).
- [A] Dataset could be misused to train exploit-seeking models (p. 12).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] No non-LLM baseline at all (no SAST tool, no fine-tuned DL/PLM model, no single-prompt LLM). The paper therefore cannot say whether the multi-agent design helps or hurts, nor how LLMs compare with traditional tools. Based on §3/§5 above (p. 7, p. 8).
- [I] The statement-level recall in Table 3 appears not to follow the stated definition. Reconstructing integer counts from Table 3 and the flag counts on p. 13 (e.g. Claude: 215 flagged, 90 function-level TP, 119 positives, 33 statement-level TP) reproduces every reported statement-level recall exactly as TP_stat / (TP_stat + function-level FN). This means "right function, wrong reasoning" cases were not counted as FN, contrary to the definition on p. 7. Under the stated definition Claude's statement-level recall would be about 27.7% (33/119), not 53.23%, and F1 about 19.8%, not 23.83%. Same pattern for all five models (GPT-4.1 ≈ 26.1% vs. 49.21%). This is our arithmetic on the paper's tables (p. 8, p. 13). It makes the headline numbers optimistic, not pessimistic.
- [I] The implied number of vulnerable functions differs by model (119-126) although the paper says 120 of 300 are vulnerable (p. 13). This suggests unreported exclusions (e.g. failed outputs) per model. Same reconstruction as above.
- [I] The detection evaluation uses only 300 functions (about 1.2% of the benchmark), drawn from Top-25 CWEs only, with no uncertainty reported. Differences of a few points between models (e.g. Claude vs. GPT-4.1, 23.83% vs. 22.38%) are within likely sampling noise (p. 8).
- [I] Circularity in Experiment 2: the "ground truth" context was generated by GPT-4.1 (p. 6), and GPT-4.1 is also one of the evaluated models (p. 9). This makes the context accuracies hard to interpret.
- [I] Task setup differs from SAST use: the pipeline gets one function plus LLM-requested definitions, not the whole repository or build. Results describe LLM function-level review, not project-scale scanning.
- [I] Class balance in the 300-sample set (40% vulnerable) is far from real codebases, so the reported precision would likely drop further in deployment. This rests on the 120/300 count (p. 13).
- [I] Data contamination is not discussed: CVEs up to 2024 and public fixes may be in the training data of all five models (no time-split analysis).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal: manual judging rules are lenient (sink-only counts as TP; up to two extra statements allowed) (p. 8); rater count and agreement not reported; the recall computation inconsistency (§9). Label noise is reduced by heuristics but not measured for the vulnerability labels themselves; only the context labels were validated (p. 5, p. 6).
- External: C/C++ only; Linux is a large share (2,793 of 10,998 vulnerable functions) (p. 5); evaluation limited to Top-25 CWEs and 300 samples (p. 8); five specific LLM versions at temperature 0.1 (p. 8).
- Construct: "correct reasoning" is a human judgement with no stated protocol beyond the four rules (p. 8); function-level detection judged without considering whether the stated reason is right (p. 7, p. 8).
- Statistical conclusion: single run per model, no confidence intervals or tests on Table 3; Mann-Whitney tests are run across five models without multiple-comparison correction (all p < 0.017, so likely robust) (p. 13).
- Reproducibility: dataset, code and full prompts released (p. 3, p. 14-p. 16); hardware and temperature reported (p. 8, p. 17); manual labels for the 300 samples availability not stated.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: use the statement-level and context labels to train and evaluate detection models (p. 10); explore smaller model sizes (p. 12); "advancing statement-level detection is essential" (p. 9).
- Suggested by us [I]: run SAST tools (e.g. CodeQL, Cppcheck) and fine-tuned DL detectors on the same 300-sample subset; report statement-level recall under the stated definition with confidence intervals; ablate the multi-agent pipeline vs. single prompt and with vs. without context; time-split by CVE date to check contamination.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (benchmark quality, granularity, duplication), RQ4 (C/C++, CWE-specific over-detection, function length), RQ5 (context, localisation, false positives), indirectly RQ3 (agentic LLM pipeline with AST/tree-sitter context; execution time) and RQ1 (LLM-only absolute effectiveness, no head-to-head).
- How it informs our work [I]: strong evidence that function-level LLM scores overstate real capability; when correct root cause is required, F1 drops by more than half. Useful for the "evaluation realism" argument and for CWE-level weakness (CWE-476/416/190 false alarms). It cannot answer RQ1 directly because there is no SAST or DL comparison.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | Best LLM (Claude-3.7-Sonnet, multi-agent) reaches 23.83% statement-level F1 and 53.89% function-level F1 on real C/C++ CVEs; function-level precision ≤47.41% for all 5 LLMs | p. 8 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Requiring correct vulnerable statements + reasoning cuts F1 by more than half vs. function-level labels (e.g. GPT-4.1 52.25% → 22.38%) | p. 8 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | SecVulEval: 25,440 de-duplicated C/C++ functions, 5,867 CVEs, 145 CWEs, statement-level + context labels; prior datasets have up to 18.9% duplicates | p. 3, p. 6 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Statement-level recall appears computed without counting wrong-reasoning cases as FN; under the stated definition Claude's recall would be ~27.7%, not 53.23% | p. 7, p. 8, p. 13 | I | moderate |
| RQ4 | All 5 LLMs detect short functions and miss long ones (median 14-33 vs. 64-71 LoC; Mann-Whitney p ≤ 0.0168) | p. 13 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | GPT-4.1 and Claude over-flag CWE-476, CWE-416 and CWE-190 (e.g. null deref despite explicit null check) | p. 13 | A | weak |
| RQ5 | LLMs identify required context poorly (≤41.33% per type; function arguments ≤5.31%; environment context 0%) | p. 9 | V | moderate |
| RQ3 | Multi-agent pipeline with open 22-33B models costs ~5-8 min per function on 4 x L40S | p. 17 | V | moderate |

## 14. Key quotes
> "The best-performing Claude-3.7-Sonnet model achieves 23.83% F1-score for detecting vulnerable statements with correct reasoning, with GPT-4.1 closely behind." (p. 1)
> "If the model correctly identifies a function as vulnerable, but the reasoning is incorrect, we consider this a True Positive for function-level detection but a False Negative for statement-level detection" (p. 7)
> "every model is significantly more successful at recognizing vulnerabilities in compact, shorter functions and consistently misses them in the longer ones." (p. 13)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: whole preprint read (pp. 1-17), including appendices A-E (limitations, failure analysis, prompts, execution time). References skimmed.
- Version / identity: `metadata.json` describes the AIware 2026 proceedings paper "SecVulEval: Context-Aware Benchmarking of LLMs for Vulnerability Detection" (DOI 10.1145/3805760.3814932). The PDF is arXiv 2505.19828v1 with title "SecVulEval: Benchmarking LLMs for Real-World C/C++ Vulnerability Detection" and the same five authors (Ahmed, Shiri Harzevili, Shin, Pham, Wang; York University) — confirmed on PDF p. 1. rlab flagged identity UNCONFIRMED only because of the title change. This analysis is based on the preprint; numbers in the published version may differ. If the published version becomes accessible, re-check Table 3 and the recall definition.
- Uncertainties: (1) The Table 3 reconstruction (§9) uses the smallest integer counts consistent with all reported percentages and with the flagged counts on p. 13. It matches all 30 percentages, but it is still our inference, not something the authors state. (2) The definition of non-vulnerable functions (fixed versions vs. unrelated functions) is not explicit. (3) The Appendix lists Qwen as "Qwen2.5-Coder-33B" (p. 13) while elsewhere it is 32B (p. 8). This is a typo-level inconsistency. (4) Our reconstruction implies Qwen flagged 124, not 121 as stated on p. 13.
- Tier: published (AIware 2026, peer-reviewed conference), but the analysed text is the not-peer-reviewed preprint.

> Version note: the text analysed is the arXiv preprint 2505.19828v1 (26 May 2025), titled "SecVulEval: Benchmarking LLMs for Real-World C/C++ Vulnerability Detection", marked "Preprint. Under review." (p. 1). The published AIware 2026 version may differ in title, numbers and content. See Analyst notes.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Build a C/C++ vulnerability benchmark with statement-level labels, rich metadata and program context (function arguments, external functions, type declarations, globals, execution environment), and use it to test how well current LLMs detect and localise real vulnerabilities (p. 1, p. 2).
- [A] Motivation: existing datasets (BigVul, CVEFixes, DiverseVul, PrimeVul, MegaVul, etc.) are function-level only, lack context, contain duplicates/mislabels, and line-level labels (BigVul, CVEFixes, SVEN) are line fragments rather than statements (p. 2, p. 3).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- No formal RQs or hypotheses. Two experiments: (1) LLM vulnerability detection at function and statement level; (2) LLM identification of the context needed for detection (p. 6, p. 7).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: benchmark construction from NVD + GitHub commits, followed by an empirical evaluation of 5 LLMs inside a multi-agent pipeline, with manual judging of statement-level outputs (p. 4-p. 8).
- Approach / model / intervention: five-agent pipeline: Normalization Agent (tree-sitter AST, no LLM), Planning Agent (function summary + checklist of up to 8 red-flag cues), Context Agent (asks for up to 6 external symbols per round, max 3 rounds; definitions fetched with tree-sitter), Detection Agent (verdict + vulnerable statements + reason), Validation Agent (agrees or disagrees; Detection reruns up to 3 times) (p. 7, p. 14-p. 16). [A] Authors claim it is the first LLM multi-agent pipeline applied to vulnerability detection (p. 7).
- Models: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, Deepseek-Coder-33B-Instruct, Codestral-22B-v0.1 (open weights, HuggingFace), GPT-4.1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet (p. 8).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: only the 5 LLMs are compared. No static-analysis tool, no fine-tuned DL/PLM detector, no single-LLM (non-agent) baseline, and no with/without-context ablation for detection (not reported).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): NVD CVEs (non-REJECTED) for products previously identified as C/C++ in BigVul, CVEFixes and PrimeVul, plus NVD keyword search ("C++", "C language", ".cpp"); only CVEs with an NVD "Patch" reference to a commit in the original (non-forked) repository; commit data via GitHub REST API (p. 4).
- Sampling / selection method: non-C/C++ files removed; only single-commit fixes kept (43 multi-commit CVEs dropped); files with no function changes removed; tangled changes filtered by keeping only functions solely modified in a file or named in the CVE/commit message; de-duplication by md5 of whitespace-normalised function text (p. 5). Detection experiment: 300 functions randomly selected from the Top-25 CWE types, manually validated; 120 of them vulnerable (p. 8, p. 12, p. 13).
- Sample size (N) and unit: 25,440 functions = 10,998 vulnerable + 14,442 non-vulnerable; 5,867 CVEs, 707 projects, 145 CWEs, CVEs from 1999-2024 (p. 6, p. 9). Function size 4-541 lines (2.5-97.5 percentile), median 44 lines; on average about 4 statements deleted and 6 added per function (p. 6). Linux alone contributes 1,920 CVEs and 2,793 vulnerable functions (p. 5).
- Non-vulnerable functions: the exact definition (fixed versions of vulnerable functions vs. other unchanged functions) is not stated explicitly. The text says both "vulnerable version" and "fixed version" copies are kept for each changed function (p. 5).
- Context labels: generated automatically by GPT-4.1 from CWE, function body, patch, commit message and CVE description. A manual check of 100 random samples (4 excluded as N/A) gave 82.98 ± 9.68% accuracy (99% CI) (p. 6).
- Data availability: dataset on HuggingFace (arag0rn/SecVulEval) and code on GitHub (basimbd/SecVulEval) (p. 3); "friendly license" for research and commercial use (p. 12).

## 5. Experimental setup

3. ## 12. Relevance to our research
