> Version note: the text analysed is the arXiv preprint 2505.19828v1 (26 May 2025), titled "SecVulEval: Benchmarking LLMs for Real-World C/C++ Vulnerability Detection", marked "Preprint. Under review." (p. 1). The published AIware 2026 version may differ in title, numbers and content. See Analyst notes.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Build a C/C++ vulnerability benchmark with statement-level labels, rich metadata and program context (function arguments, external functions, type declarations, globals, execution environment), and use it to test how well current LLMs detect and localise real vulnerabilities (p. 1, p. 2).
- [A] Motivation: existing datasets (BigVul, CVEFixes, DiverseVul, PrimeVul, MegaVul, etc.) are function-level only, lack context, contain duplicates/mislabels, and line-level labels (BigVul, CVEFixes, SVEN) are line fragments rather than statements (p. 2, p. 3).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- No formal RQs or hypotheses. Two experiments: (1) LLM vulnerability detection at function and statement level; (2) LLM identification of the context needed for detection (p. 6, p. 7).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: benchmark construction from NVD + GitHub commits, followed by an empirical evaluation of 5 LLMs inside a multi-agent pipeline, with manual judging of statement-level outputs (p. 4-p. 8).
- Approach / model / intervention: five-agent pipeline: Normalization Agent (tree-sitter AST, no LLM), Planning Agent (function summary + checklist of up to 8 red-flag cues), Context Agent (asks for up to 6 external symbols per round, max 3 rounds; definitions fetched with tree-sitter), Detection Agent (verdict + vulnerable statements + reason), Validation Agent (agrees or disagrees; Detection reruns up to 3 times) (p. 7, p. 14-p. 16). [A] Authors claim it is the first LLM multi-agent pipeline applied to vulnerability detection (p. 7).
- Models: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, Deepseek-Coder-33B-Instruct, Codestral-22B-v0.1 (open weights, HuggingFace), GPT-4.1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet (p. 8).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: only the 5 LLMs are compared. No static-analysis tool, no fine-tuned DL/PLM detector, no single-LLM (non-agent) baseline, and no with/without-context ablation for detection (not reported).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): NVD CVEs (non-REJECTED) for products previously identified as C/C++ in BigVul, CVEFixes and PrimeVul, plus NVD keyword search ("C++", "C language", ".cpp"); only CVEs with an NVD "Patch" reference to a commit in the original (non-forked) repository; commit data via GitHub REST API (p. 4).
- Sampling / selection method: non-C/C++ files removed; only single-commit fixes kept (43 multi-commit CVEs dropped); files with no function changes removed; tangled changes filtered by keeping only functions solely modified in a file or named in the CVE/commit message; de-duplication by md5 of whitespace-normalised function text (p. 5). Detection experiment: 300 functions randomly selected from the Top-25 CWE types, manually validated; 120 of them vulnerable (p. 8, p. 12, p. 13).
- Sample size (N) and unit: 25,440 functions = 10,998 vulnerable + 14,442 non-vulnerable; 5,867 CVEs, 707 projects, 145 CWEs, CVEs from 1999-2024 (p. 6, p. 9). Function size 4-541 lines (2.5-97.5 percentile), median 44 lines; on average about 4 statements deleted and 6 added per function (p. 6). Linux alone contributes 1,920 CVEs and 2,793 vulnerable functions (p. 5).
- Non-vulnerable functions: the exact definition (fixed versions of vulnerable functions vs. other unchanged functions) is not stated explicitly. The text says both "vulnerable version" and "fixed version" copies are kept for each changed function (p. 5).
- Context labels: generated automatically by GPT-4.1 from CWE, function body, patch, commit message and CVE description. A manual check of 100 random samples (4 excluded as N/A) gave 82.98 ± 9.68% accuracy (99% CI) (p. 6).
- Data availability: dataset on HuggingFace (arag0rn/SecVulEval) and code on GitHub (basimbd/SecVulEval) (p. 3); "friendly license" for research and commercial use (p. 12).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: pass@1, temperature 0.1; Intel Xeon Gold 6442Y CPU, 4 x NVIDIA L40S GPUs, 250 GiB RAM; open models via transformers.pipeline (p. 8, p. 17). Prompts for all four LLM agents are given verbatim. They were rewritten to stress *defensive* research after models refused to answer (p. 13-p. 16). Function and AST inputs "could be truncated if too long" (p. 14); the truncation limit is not reported.
- Statement-level TP rules (manual): exact vulnerable statements with correct reasoning; or at least one of several fix locations; or correct statements plus at most two unrelated ones; or only the sink statement / sink + source with correct reasoning (p. 8). Function level is judged automatically from the `is_vulnerable` field (p. 8).
- Number and independence of manual raters, and inter-rater agreement: not reported.
- Cost/time: open models take 4.97-7.99 minutes per function in total (Codestral 4.97, Qwen 6.03, Deepseek 7.99) (p. 17). Time for the proprietary models and API cost are not reported (p. 17).
- Code availability: GitHub repository (p. 3).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: precision, recall and F1 at function level (is the function vulnerable?) and statement level (are the vulnerable statements identified with correct reasoning?). A function-level TP with wrong reasoning is defined as a statement-level FN (p. 7). Context identification: accuracy per context type versus dataset ground truth, which is itself GPT-4.1-generated (p. 6, p. 7, p. 9).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): one-sided Mann-Whitney U tests compare the function length of detected vs. missed vulnerable functions (p. 12, p. 13). The detection metrics have no confidence intervals or significance tests, and repeated runs are not reported.

## 7. Key findings
1. Statement-level detection is poor for all models: F1 = Claude-3.7-Sonnet 23.83%, GPT-4.1 22.38%, Codestral-22B 15.31%, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B 13.57%, Deepseek-Coder-33B 7.14% — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
2. Function-level F1: Claude 53.89%, GPT-4.1 52.25%, Codestral 46.61%, Deepseek 45.71%, Qwen 35.20%. Function-level precision is only 35.48-47.41% for every model — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
3. The proprietary models are more "aggressive": function-level recall is 75.63% (Claude) and 73.11% (GPT-4.1), but precision is 41.86% and 40.65%, lower than Codestral (47.41%) and Deepseek (45.16%). Of 300 samples (120 vulnerable), GPT-4.1 and Claude flagged 214 and 215 as vulnerable vs. 116-124 for the open models — [V] (p. 8, p. 13).
4. Statement-level precision is 5.65-15.35% for all models, i.e. most flagged statements/reasons are wrong — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
5. Detected vulnerable functions are much shorter than missed ones: median 14-33 LoC detected vs. 64-71 LoC missed; one-sided Mann-Whitney U p = 0.000197-0.0168 for all five models — [V] (p. 12, p. 13, Table 5).
6. Over-detection concentrates on CWE-476 (NULL dereference, flagged even when an explicit null check exists), CWE-416 (any `free()`/`kfree()` treated as use-after-free) and CWE-190 (arithmetic flagged as overflow without analysis), especially for GPT-4.1 and Claude. This is qualitative, from manual validation; no counts are given — [A] (p. 13).
7. LLMs identify the needed context poorly. The best per type is Claude (external functions 37.00%, type definitions 41.33%, globals 34.53%). Function-argument accuracy is 0-5.31% for all models, and no model identified any environment-level context (1.5% of all contexts) — [V] (p. 9, Table 4).
8. GPT-4.1 identifies the required context with 82.98 ± 9.68% accuracy when given the patch, CVE and commit message. This is the dataset-construction setting, not detection — [V] (p. 6).
9. SecVulEval has 0.0% duplicates vs. 18.9% (CVEFixes), 12.7% (BigVul) and 3.3% (DiverseVul) as reported by PrimeVul. The SecVulEval figure is the authors' own; the others are cited from their ref. [5] — [V] (p. 3, Table 1).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Context labels were produced by an LLM; manual validation covered only 100 samples; "relevant context" is subjective; repository-wide / transitive context is not covered (p. 12).
- [A] Manual statement-level judging is subjective and labour-intensive, which limits scale (p. 12).
- [A] Only the largest runnable size of each model was evaluated; conclusions may not hold for smaller sizes (p. 12).
- [A] Multi-commit fixes were excluded for simplicity (p. 5).
- [A] The dataset could be misused to train models to exploit vulnerabilities (p. 12).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] There is no non-LLM baseline at all (no SAST tool, no fine-tuned DL/PLM model, no single-prompt LLM). So the paper cannot say whether the multi-agent design helps or hurts, or how LLMs compare with traditional tools. Based on §3/§5 above.
- [I] The statement-level recall in Table 3 appears not to follow the stated definition. We reconstructed integer counts from Table 3 and the flag counts on p. 13 (e.g. Claude: 215 flagged, 90 function-level TP, 119 positives, 33 statement-level TP). Every reported statement-level recall is reproduced exactly as TP_stat / (TP_stat + function-level FN). That means "right function, wrong reasoning" cases were not counted as FN, contrary to the definition on p. 7. Under the stated definition, Claude's statement-level recall would be about 27.7% (33/119), not 53.23%, and its F1 about 19.8%, not 23.83%. The same pattern holds for all five models (GPT-4.1: about 26.1% vs. 49.21%). This is our arithmetic on the paper's tables (p. 8, p. 13). It makes the headline numbers optimistic, not pessimistic.
- [I] The implied number of vulnerable functions differs by model (119-126), although the paper says 120 of 300 are vulnerable (p. 13). This suggests unreported per-model exclusions (e.g. failed outputs). Same reconstruction as above.
- [I] The detection evaluation uses only 300 functions (about 1.2% of the benchmark), drawn from Top-25 CWEs only, with no uncertainty reported. Gaps of a few points between models (e.g. Claude vs. GPT-4.1, 23.83% vs. 22.38%) are probably within sampling noise. Based on p. 8.
- [I] Experiment 2 is circular: the context "ground truth" was generated by GPT-4.1 (p. 6), and GPT-4.1 is also one of the evaluated models (p. 9). This makes the context accuracies hard to interpret.
- [I] The task differs from SAST use. The pipeline gets one function plus LLM-requested definitions, not the whole repository or build. The results describe LLM review of single functions, not project-scale scanning.
- [I] The 300-sample set is 40% vulnerable, far more than in real codebases, so precision would likely drop further in deployment. This rests on the 120/300 count (p. 13).
- [I] Data contamination is not discussed: CVEs up to 2024 and their public fixes may be in the training data of all five models, and there is no time-split analysis.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): the manual judging rules are lenient (sink-only counts as TP; up to two extra statements allowed) (p. 8). The number of raters and their agreement are not reported. There is also the recall inconsistency in §9. Heuristics reduce label noise, but noise in the vulnerability labels is never measured; only the context labels were validated (p. 5, p. 6). De-duplication removes exact duplicates only (p. 5).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): C/C++ only. Linux is a large share (2,793 of 10,998 vulnerable functions) (p. 5). The evaluation covers only Top-25 CWEs and 300 samples (p. 8), and five specific LLM versions at temperature 0.1 (p. 8).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): "correct reasoning" is a human judgement with no stated protocol beyond the four rules (p. 8). Function-level detection is judged without checking whether the stated reason is right (p. 7, p. 8).

Best F1 is UniXcoder 0.4626 (MCC 0.3495); CodeT5P has the highest MCC 0.3627; GPT-4o ITFSP reaches F1 0.4010, MCC 0.2774. The authors conclude the PLM "remains superior in overall classification balance" in the imbalanced setting — [V] (p. 40, p. 41). Instruction-tuned GPT-4o zero-shot has P 0.9659 but R 0.0834 — [V] (p. 40).

It is best on 23 of 25 CWEs (CodeT5P leads or ties on 7); e.g. CWE-787 82.93% vs 56.1%, CWE-79 78.28% vs 63.13%, CWE-89 78.26% vs 58.7% — [V] (p. 29, p. 30, Table 5).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Only the REEF dataset and seven languages; generalisation to other languages is unknown (p. 43).
- [A] The 512-token limit of the PLMs restricts context for longer code (p. 43).
- [A] Single-language specialised LLM detectors (mostly C/C++) are excluded, which limits comparison with customised tools (p. 43).
- [A] Tree-sitter may misidentify functions (sanity check done) (p. 43).
- [A] Leakage from the same project/developer across splits is possible; only exact-match filtering is applied (p. 44).
- [A] Tangled commits add label noise; heuristics reduce it, but line-level manual verification is future work (p. 44).
- [A] Reasoning LLMs were not fine-tuned with RL (p. 38).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **No static-analysis tool is compared.** For our RQ1, this paper supports only LLM-vs-DL/PLM claims, not LLM-vs-SAST. Based on §3 (p. 9-p. 11).
- [I] **The headline result rests on one configuration.** GPT-4o ITFSP is the only LLM setting clearly above chance at function level (next best 0.5874). Few-shot hurts every other model, and the paper gives no explanation, ablation, seed variation or test. A single strong outlier without variance estimates is fragile. Based on Table 3 (p. 17).
- [I] **Possible leakage via paired functions and BM25 retrieval.** The split is random at function level (p. 7), and each vulnerable function has its fixed twin labelled clean (p. 6). Twins and functions from the same CVE/project can fall on opposite sides of the split, and BM25 few-shot retrieval from the training set could then return a near-identical twin with the opposite label. Only exact-match filtering is applied (p. 44). This could favour the few-shot + fine-tuned setting. It is a hypothesis only; the paper gives no retrieval-overlap statistics. The time-split check (p. 38) tests memorisation of pre-training data, not this split-level overlap.
- [I] **Line-level accuracy/FPR are probably inflated by padding.** The DummyClf_vul precision on the line-level test set is 0.0267 (p. 23), i.e. 2.67% vulnerable lines. But Table 2 implies about 14.3% vulnerable lines (25,161 / 175,768) (p. 8). 810 test functions x 113 padded line slots ≈ 91,530 slots, and 2.67% of that ≈ 2,440 vulnerable lines, close to the ≈2,500 expected from the dataset average (3.1 per function). This suggests metrics are computed over padded 113-line slots. If so, accuracy (≈0.95-0.98) and FPR are inflated and not comparable to other papers. F1/precision/recall are less affected. Our arithmetic, unconfirmed by the authors.
- [I] The line-level task is easier than real use: only known-vulnerable functions are given, the LLM prompt says the function is vulnerable (p. 11), and only functions with deleted lines are kept (p. 7).
- [I] Short functions only: functions over 512 tokens are removed (p. 6), and median LOC in the divergent samples is 9-36 (p. 33). Scale effects (RQ4) are not tested.
- [I] The 2024-2025 time-split accuracy (0.7874) is higher than in-distribution (0.7196) (p. 39, p. 17). This is unusual and unexplained. Line-level F1 halves (0.6641 → 0.3450), which suggests that localisation does not generalise well over time (p. 39).
- [I] Text vs. table mismatches: CodeBERT Acc 0.5163 in the text vs 0.5173 in the table (p. 18 vs p. 17); GPT-3.5 zero-shot 0.4758 vs 0.4827 (p. 19 vs p. 17); UniXcoder MCC 0.3475 vs 0.3495 (p. 41 vs p. 40); GPT-4o imbalanced zero-shot F1 "0.1264" in the text vs 0.2036 in the table (p. 40). The model is called "GPT-4" in places (p. 21, p. 38). Minor issues, but signs of limited proofreading.
- [I] The per-CWE "correct detection" percentage mixes vulnerable and clean items. At line level, what counts as "correct" for a function is not defined (p. 29, p. 30).
- [I] Pooled metrics are dominated by JavaScript (548 of 2,026 function-level test items) (p. 7, p. 15). C# results rest on 44 / 13 test functions (p. 7, p. 8).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): random function-level split, not split by CVE, project or time (p. 7); possible twin/BM25 leakage (§9); possible padding effect on line-level metrics (§9); PLMs are reproduced from original hyper-parameters, while LLM prompt templates differ across strategies (p. 11, p. 13, p. 43).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): REEF only; seven languages; short functions (≤512 tokens) (p. 6, p. 43); balanced test (50/50) by default (p. 7). The imbalanced variant (p. 39) changes the conclusion.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): the line-level task presupposes a known-vulnerable function (p. 11). Labels come from fix commits (pre-change = vulnerable, post-change = clean) with known tangling noise (p. 6, p. 44). The authors report that two raters judged 92-93% of 377 extracted functions correct (p. 7).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no tests, confidence intervals or seeds. Many configurations (≈30) are compared on one split, and the best is chosen post hoc. Per-language and per-CWE cells are small (e.g. C# 44/13; CWE-862 n = 1) (p. 7, p. 8, p. 30).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): data and scripts are released (p. 48), and model versions are given for the OpenAI models (p. 15). Hyper-parameters, decoding settings and GPT fine-tuning details are not in the paper (p. 16).
- Funding: Chinese and Japanese public grants; no conflict of interest declared (p. 48).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: larger multilingual benchmarks; intermediate representations that unify code across languages; better PLM/LLM learning strategies such as multi-task learning or meta-learning to close the gap between high- and low-resource languages (p. 47); RL fine-tuning of reasoning LLMs (p. 38); line-level manual verification of labels (p. 44); adding specialised models as they support more languages (p. 43).
- Suggested by us [I]: add SAST baselines (CodeQL/Semgrep) on the same multilingual test split; split by CVE/project/time; repeat the GPT-4o ITFSP run with several seeds and BM25-overlap controls; compute line-level metrics on real lines only; evaluate realistic class ratios as the main setting.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (LLM vs DL/PLM head-to-head; no SAST), RQ2 (balanced vs imbalanced reversal; time split; pooled metrics; line-level setup), RQ3 (cost/TCO of API LLM vs local PLM; no hybrid), RQ4 (per-language, per-CWE, per-severity, function complexity), RQ5 (leakage, granularity, imbalance).
- How it informs our work [I]: one of the few multilingual, two-granularity LLM-vs-PLM comparisons. Its main lesson for the review is conditional: only a fine-tuned frontier LLM with retrieved examples beats fine-tuned PLMs, and only on balanced data. Under realistic imbalance, fine-tuned PLMs match or beat it. Prompt-only LLMs are near chance at function level. This supports a "results depend on setup" answer to RQ2.

## 14. Key quotes
> "GPT-4o with instruction tuning and few-shot prompting demonstrates superior performance, achieving the highest accuracy (0.7196) at function-level compared to the best-performing CodeT5P (0.6037)" (p. 4)

> "the PLM remains superior in overall classification balance for this imbalanced dataset." (p. 41)

> "the size of LLMs is not the decisive factor affecting performance on multilingual vulnerability detection, and the use of reasoning LLMs does not lead to significant improvements." (p. 4)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: pp. 1-48 read in full (all sections, tables 1-12, threats, conclusion, declarations). The reference list (pp. 48-53) was skimmed. Figures 4, 5 and 8-10 are bar charts garbled by text extraction; we rely on the numbers the authors give in the text for them (p. 21, p. 26, p. 32, p. 34).
- Version: metadata = EMSE 2026 (DOI 10.1007/s10664-026-10832-4). The analysed text is arXiv 2506.07503v2 (10 Mar 2026), identity matched by arXiv id. The typeset journal version may differ slightly. The running header reads "W. Dong et al.", a template artifact.
- Uncertainties: (1) The padding hypothesis and the twin/BM25 leakage hypothesis (§9) are our inference from reported numbers; the replication package could settle both. - RQ1: How effective are PLMs and LLMs at detecting multilingual vulnerabilities at function level? (p. 4)
- RQ2: ... at line level? (p. 4)
- RQ3: What are the strengths and weaknesses of PLMs and LLMs in multilingual detection? (p. 4)
- Discussion experiments: code-structure analysis, model size (70B), reasoning LLMs, time-split leakage check, imbalanced setting, deployment cost (p. 32-p. 43).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: controlled empirical comparison on a fixed random 8:1:1 split, stratified by language, of the REEF dataset (p. 7, p. 8).
- Approach / model / intervention:
  - PLMs (function level): CodeBERT, CodeT5, CodeT5P, UniXcoder and LineVul, fully fine-tuned with an MLP head on the [CLS] token. OpenAI Text-Embedding-Ada-002 / 3-Small / 3-Large are used as frozen encoders with a trained classifier head (p. 9, p. 16).
  - PLMs (line level): CodeBERT, UniXcoder, CodeT5, CodeT5P, with up to 113 lines x 31 tokens per function, GRU per line, per-line sigmoid, threshold 0.5. LineVul and the embedding models are excluded at line level (p. 22).
  - LLMs: DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B, Code Llama 7B, Llama 3 8B (HuggingFace), GPT-3.5-Turbo (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125), GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) (p. 10, p. 15). Strategies: zero-shot; few-shot with 3 BM25-retrieved training examples; instruction tuning (LoRA) followed by zero-shot or few-shot prompting (p. 12, p. 14). GRACE (AST-enhanced LLM, zero-shot) is added as a baseline at function level (p. 10, p. 11).
  - Line-level LLM prompts state that the function is vulnerable, and lines are tagged "Line N:" (p. 11, p. 23).
  - Extra models: Code Llama 70B and Llama 3 70B (p. 35); reasoning LLMs DeepSeek-R1 (671B) and QwQ-plus, zero-shot only (p. 37).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: dummy classifiers that predict all-vulnerable or all-clean (p. 11). **No static-analysis (SAST) tool and no GNN/RNN detector is evaluated.** GNNs/RNNs are excluded because ASTs are language-specific and PLMs were previously shown to be better (p. 9, p. 10). MSIVD and Vul-RAG are excluded for lack of multilingual knowledge/explanations (p. 11).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): REEF (Wang et al. 2023a): 4,466 CVEs, 30,987 patches, NVD + Mend CVE list, 2016-2023, seven languages (p. 6).
- Sampling / selection method: comments removed; functions extracted with Tree-sitter; the pre-change function is labelled vulnerable and the post-change function clean (matched by name, then by edit distance); functions longer than 512 removed (PLM input limit) (p. 6). Line labels come from deleted lines (difflib); vulnerable functions fixed by additions only are dropped (p. 6, p. 7). Split: 8:1:1 stratified random sampling per language (p. 7, p. 8). "Exact-match filtering" against leakage (p. 44).
- Sample size (N) and unit:
  - Function level: 20,165 functions (10,133 vulnerable / 10,032 clean); train 16,126 / val 2,013 / test 2,026. Per language: C 3,056; C++ 1,792; C# 427; Go 2,905; Java 3,235; JavaScript 5,468; Python 3,282. Test sets per language: C 307, C++ 181, C# 44, Go 292, Java 325, JavaScript 548, Python 329 (p. 7, Table 1).
  - Line level: 8,134 vulnerable functions (train 6,513 / val 811 / test 810); 25,161 vulnerable vs 150,607 non-vulnerable lines. C# test set has only 13 functions (p. 8, Table 2).
  - Tree-sitter extraction check: 377 random samples, 93% / 92% judged correct by two authors, Cohen's kappa 0.9448 (p. 7).
  - Severity: 1.2% low, 41.12% high, 25.09% critical (CVSS v4.0) (p. 8).
  - Time-split set (2024-2025, same pipeline): 3,138 function-level samples (balanced) and 1,328 line-level samples (p. 38).
  - Imbalanced set (benign functions mined from unchanged functions): train 48,219 / val 6,012 / test 6,051; test = 1,019 vulnerable + 5,032 benign (p. 39).
- Data availability (public? link?): data, training and evaluation scripts on GitHub (SpanShu96/Large-Language-Model-for-Multilingual-Vulnerability-Detection) (p. 48).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: PLMs replicated following Steenhoek et al. 2024a, using the original authors' hyper-parameters (p. 15, p. 43). LoRA for instruction tuning (p. 14, p. 16). Hardware: Xeon Gold 6342, 512 GB RAM, 2 x A800 GPUs (p. 16). Detailed hyper-parameters (learning rate, epochs, LoRA rank, temperature/decoding) are not reported in the paper; it refers to the replication package (p. 16). How GPT-3.5/GPT-4o were instruction-tuned is not described explicitly, but Table 12 lists per-token training costs for them (p. 41).
- Metrics are pooled over all test samples across languages, not averaged per language (p. 15).
- Code availability: yes (p. 48).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (binary), FPR, FNR, MCC, AUC (trapezoidal) (p. 14, p. 15). Accuracy is the primary metric at function level because the data is balanced; F1 is primary at line level because the data is imbalanced (p. 17, p. 23). RQ3 uses the share of correct detections per Top-25 CWE (2023 list) and per CVSS severity, plus Venn diagrams of unique correct/incorrect predictions (p. 27, p. 28).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): **none.** No significance tests, confidence intervals or repeated runs/seeds are reported. The words "significantly" and "significant" are used without tests (e.g. p. 21, p. 26, p. 38).

## 7. Key findings
1. Function level, balanced (Table 3): best LLM = GPT-4o with instruction tuning + few-shot (ITFSP): Acc 0.7196, P 0.7454, R 0.6722, F1 0.7069, FPR 0.2324, MCC 0.4360, AUC 0.7169. Best PLM = CodeT5P: Acc 0.6037, P 0.5626, R 0.9529, F1 0.7075, FPR 0.7496, MCC 0.2860, AUC 0.6015 — [V] (p. 17). F1 is essentially tied (0.7069 vs 0.7075); the gap is in accuracy/precision/FPR/MCC.
2. Every other LLM configuration at function level is near chance: zero-shot accuracy 0.4827-0.5061 (GRACE 0.5061), MCC −0.0585 to 0.0244; few-shot without tuning lowers accuracy for all but GPT-4o (e.g. GPT-3.5 0.3618, DeepSeek-Coder 0.3870); best instruction-tuned zero-shot is GPT-4o at 0.5874 — [V] (p. 17, p. 19).
3. Text-embedding models, CodeBERT and LineVul are near random at function level (Acc 0.5030-0.5173, AUC 0.50-0.51; LineVul and CodeBERT rows identical) — [V] (p. 17).
4. Per language, function level (Acc): GPT-4o ITFSP — C 0.7557, C# 0.7273, C++ 0.7901, Go 0.8082, JavaScript 0.6642, Java 0.7169, Python 0.6626. CodeT5P — C 0.5081, C# 0.6136, C++ 0.5249, Go 0.6062, JavaScript 0.7062, Java 0.6031, Python 0.5623 — [V] (p. 21). In JavaScript, CodeT5P (0.7062) and CodeT5 (0.6898) beat GPT-4o (0.6642). This contradicts the claim that GPT-4o "outperformed all other PLMs and LLMs across all seven studied languages" (p. 22) — [V] (p. 21, p. 22).
5. Line level (Table 4): GPT-4o ITFSP F1 0.6641 (P 0.7012, R 0.6307, MCC 0.6563, AUC 0.8116) vs best PLM CodeT5P F1 0.4841 (P 0.3536, R 0.7673, MCC 0.5029, AUC 0.8644). GPT-4o few-shot without tuning already gives F1 0.6050. Zero-shot LLM F1 is 0.2254-0.3313 — [V] (p. 23, p. 25, p. 26). CodeT5P has the higher AUC — [V] (p. 26).
6. Per language, line level (F1): GPT-4o ITFSP — C 0.5478, C# 0.4348, C++ 0.5774, Go 0.7078, JavaScript 0.7815, Java 0.6391, Python 0.6055. CodeT5P — C 0.3727, C# 0.4750, C++ 0.4768, Go 0.4146, JavaScript 0.6556, Java 0.4167, Python 0.4519 — [V] (p. 26). CodeT5P wins in C# (13 test functions) — [V] (p. 8, p. 26).
7. Imbalanced function-level setting (~17% vulnerable; Table 11): the ranking reverses. Best F1 is UniXcoder 0.4626 (MCC 0.3495); CodeT5P has the highest MCC 0.3627; GPT-4o ITFSP reaches F1 0.4010, MCC 0.2774. The authors conclude the PLM "remains superior in overall classification balance" in the imbalanced setting — [V] (p. 40, p. 41). Instruction-tuned GPT-4o zero-shot has P 0.9659 but R 0.0834 — [V] (p. 40).
8. Top-25 CWEs (function level, per-CWE accuracy over vulnerable + clean functions, 1,119 test items): GPT-4o ITFSP 75.87% vs CodeT5P 61.13%. It is best on 23 of 25 CWEs (CodeT5P leads or ties on 7); e.g. CWE-787 82.93% vs 56.1%, CWE-79 78.28% vs 63.13%, CWE-89 78.26% vs 58.7% — [V] (p. 29, p. 30, Table 5).
9. Top-25 CWEs (line level, 441 items): GPT-4o ITFSP 50.79% vs CodeT5P 21.77%. Memory-safety CWEs are hardest: CWE-787 1/16 (6.25%), CWE-119 21.74%, CWE-125 27.27% — [V] (p. 30, Table 6). The authors find 11 CWEs, including CWE-787, CWE-125 and CWE-22, are "detected" at function level but not at line level — [A] (p. 31).
10. Severity: at function level GPT-4o ITFSP has 630 correct High-severity detections vs CodeT5P 514, but fewer Critical (305 vs 321). At line level, 134 Critical vs 76 — [V] (p. 32).
11. Complementarity: CodeT5P has the most unique correct function-level detections (108 vs 28 for GPT-4o ITFSP), but GPT-4o ITFSP has the fewest unique incorrect detections (11 vs 136) — [V] (p. 29). In 608 LLM-only-correct vs 370 PLM-only-correct functions, the LLM-only set has higher median cyclomatic complexity (4.0 vs 2.0), tokens (135.5 vs 96.0) and LOC (19 vs 15), but lower nesting (2.0 vs 3.0) — [V] (p. 32, p. 34).
12. Model size: 70B Code Llama / Llama 3 bring no function-level gain (accuracies 0.4659-0.5093). At line level, Llama 3 70B few-shot F1 is 0.5214 vs 0.2822 for 8B, while Code Llama 70B gets worse (0.2267 vs 0.3257) — [V] (p. 35, p. 36).
13. Reasoning LLMs (zero-shot): DeepSeek-R1 Acc 0.5217 / line F1 0.2746; QwQ-plus Acc 0.5346 / line F1 0.3136. Only slightly above random, and not better than non-reasoning LLMs at line level — [V] (p. 37, p. 38).
14. Time-split check (2024-2025 CVEs): GPT-4o ITFSP function-level Acc 0.7874, F1 0.7804, MCC 0.5767; line-level F1 0.3450, MCC 0.3301 (down from 0.6641 in-distribution) — [V] (p. 38, p. 39, Table 10). The authors conclude the LLM "does not merely memorize" — [A] (p. 39).
15. Cost: GPT-4o instruction tuning $86.07 (function) / $59.42 (line); inference input ≈$1.65 / $0.95 for the test set. A local A6000 PLM training run costs ≈$5.59 (≈15x cheaper), with break-even after 58 fine-tuning runs — [V] (p. 41, p. 42). The authors recommend PLMs for organisations with privacy constraints or only consumer GPUs — [A] (p. 42, p. 43).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Only the REEF dataset and seven languages; generalisation to other languages is unknown (p. 43).
- [A] The 512-token limit of the PLMs restricts context for longer code (p. 43).
- [A] Single-language specialised LLM detectors (mostly C/C++) are excluded, which limits comparison with customised tools (p. 43).
- [A] Tree-sitter may misidentify functions (sanity check done) (p. 43).
- [A] Leakage from the same project/developer across splits is possible; only exact-match filtering is applied (p. 44).
- [A] Tangled commits add label noise; heuristics reduce it, but line-level manual verification is future work (p. 44).
- [A] Reasoning LLMs were not fine-tuned with RL (p. 38).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **No static-analysis tool is compared.** For our RQ1, this paper supports only LLM-vs-DL/PLM claims, not LLM-vs-SAST. Based on §3 (p. 9-p. 11).
- [I] **The headline result rests on one configuration.** GPT-4o ITFSP is the only LLM setting clearly above chance at function level (next best 0.5874). Few-shot hurts every other model, and the paper gives no explanation, ablation, seed variation or test. A single strong outlier without variance estimates is fragile. Based on Table 3 (p. 17).
- [I] **Possible leakage via paired functions and BM25 retrieval.** The split is random at function level (p. 7), and each vulnerable function has its fixed twin labelled clean (p. 6). Twins and functions from the same CVE/project can fall on opposite sides of the split, and BM25 few-shot retrieval from the training set could then return a near-identical twin with the opposite label. Only exact-match filtering is applied (p. 44). This could favour the few-shot + fine-tuned setting. It is a hypothesis only; the paper gives no retrieval-overlap statistics. The time-split check (p. 38) tests memorisation of pre-training data, not this split-level overlap.
- [I] **Line-level accuracy/FPR are probably inflated by padding.** The DummyClf_vul precision on the line-level test set is 0.0267 (p. 23), i.e. 2.67% vulnerable lines. But Table 2 implies about 14.3% vulnerable lines (25,161 / 175,768) (p. 8). 810 test functions x 113 padded line slots ≈ 91,530 slots, and 2.67% of that ≈ 2,440 vulnerable lines, close to the ≈2,500 expected from the dataset average (3.1 per function). This suggests metrics are computed over padded 113-line slots. If so, accuracy (≈0.95-0.98) and FPR are inflated and not comparable to other papers. F1/precision/recall are less affected. Our arithmetic, unconfirmed by the authors.
- [I] The line-level task is easier than real use: only known-vulnerable functions are given, the LLM prompt says the function is vulnerable (p. 11), and only functions with deleted lines are kept (p. 7).
- [I] Short functions only: functions over 512 tokens are removed (p. 6), and median LOC in the divergent samples is 9-36 (p. 33). Scale effects (RQ4) are not tested.
- [I] The 2024-2025 time-split accuracy (0.7874) is higher than in-distribution (0.7196) (p. 39, p. 17). This is unusual and unexplained. Line-level F1 halves (0.6641 → 0.3450), which suggests that localisation does not generalise well over time (p. 39).
- [I] Text vs. table mismatches: CodeBERT Acc 0.5163 in the text vs 0.5173 in the table (p. 18 vs p. 17); GPT-3.5 zero-shot 0.4758 vs 0.4827 (p. 19 vs p. 17); UniXcoder MCC 0.3475 vs 0.3495 (p. 41 vs p. 40); GPT-4o imbalanced zero-shot F1 "0.1264" in the text vs 0.2036 in the table (p. 40). The model is called "GPT-4" in places (p. 21, p. 38). Minor issues, but signs of limited proofreading.
- [I] The per-CWE "correct detection" percentage mixes vulnerable and clean items. At line level, what counts as "correct" for a function is not defined (p. 29, p. 30).
- [I] Pooled metrics are dominated by JavaScript (548 of 2,026 function-level test items) (p. 7, p. 15). C# results rest on 44 / 13 test functions (p. 7, p. 8).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): random function-level split, not split by CVE, project or time (p. 7); possible twin/BM25 leakage (§9); possible padding effect on line-level metrics (§9); PLMs are reproduced from original hyper-parameters, while LLM prompt templates differ across strategies (p. 11, p. 13, p. 43).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): REEF only; seven languages; short functions (≤512 tokens) (p. 6, p. 43); balanced test (50/50) by default (p. 7). The imbalanced variant (p. 39) changes the conclusion.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): the line-level task presupposes a known-vulnerable function (p. 11). Labels come from fix commits (pre-change = vulnerable, post-change = clean) with known tangling noise (p. 6, p. 44). The authors report that two raters judged 92-93% of 377 extracted functions correct (p. 7).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no tests, confidence intervals or seeds. Many configurations (≈30) are compared on one split, and the best is chosen post hoc. Per-language and per-CWE cells are small (e.g. C# 44/13; CWE-862 n = 1) (p. 7, p. 8, p. 30).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): data and scripts are released (p. 48), and model versions are given for the OpenAI models (p. 15). Hyper-parameters, decoding settings and GPT fine-tuning details are not in the paper (p. 16).
- Funding: Chinese and Japanese public grants; no conflict of interest declared (p. 48).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: larger multilingual benchmarks; intermediate representations that unify code across languages; better PLM/LLM learning strategies such as multi-task learning or meta-learning to close the gap between high- and low-resource languages (p. 47); RL fine-tuning of reasoning LLMs (p. 38); line-level manual verification of labels (p. 44); adding specialised models as they support more languages (p. 43).
- Suggested by us [I]: add SAST baselines (CodeQL/Semgrep) on the same multilingual test split; split by CVE/project/time; repeat the GPT-4o ITFSP run with several seeds and BM25-overlap controls; compute line-level metrics on real lines only; evaluate realistic class ratios as the main setting.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (LLM vs DL/PLM head-to-head; no SAST), RQ2 (balanced vs imbalanced reversal; time split; pooled metrics; line-level setup), RQ3 (cost/TCO of API LLM vs local PLM; no hybrid), RQ4 (per-language, per-CWE, per-severity, function complexity), RQ5 (leakage, granularity, imbalance).
- How it informs our work [I]: one of the few multilingual, two-granularity LLM-vs-PLM comparisons. Its main lesson for the review is conditional: only a fine-tuned frontier LLM with retrieved examples beats fine-tuned PLMs, and only on balanced data. Under realistic imbalance, fine-tuned PLMs match or beat it. Prompt-only LLMs are near chance at function level. This supports a "results depend on setup" answer to RQ2.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | On balanced REEF (7 languages), fine-tuned GPT-4o + BM25 few-shot beats best PLM CodeT5P at function level (Acc 0.7196 vs 0.6037; MCC 0.4360 vs 0.2860; F1 tied 0.7069 vs 0.7075) | p. 17 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | Prompt-only LLMs (zero-/few-shot, incl. GPT-4o, GRACE, DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-plus) are near chance at function level (Acc 0.36-0.53, MCC ≤0.07) | p. 17, p. 37 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | Line level: GPT-4o ITFSP F1 0.6641 vs CodeT5P 0.4841 (but CodeT5P AUC 0.8644 > 0.8116) | p. 23, p. 26 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Under realistic imbalance (~17% vulnerable), PLMs outperform the best LLM (UniXcoder F1 0.4626 / CodeT5P MCC 0.3627 vs GPT-4o ITFSP F1 0.4010 / MCC 0.2774) — conclusion flips with class ratio | p. 40, p. 41 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Time-split (2024-2025) GPT-4o ITFSP keeps function-level Acc 0.7874 but line-level F1 drops to 0.3450 from 0.6641 | p. 39 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Random function-level split with paired vulnerable/fixed twins and BM25 few-shot retrieval from train; only exact-match dedup — possible leakage favouring ITFSP | p. 6, p. 7, p. 44 | I | weak |
| RQ2 | Line-level dummy precision 0.0267 vs ~14% vulnerable lines in dataset suggests metrics over padded 113-line slots, inflating accuracy/FPR | p. 8, p. 22, p. 23 | I | weak |
| RQ3 | GPT-4o instruction tuning costs $86.07 (function) vs ≈$5.59 per local A6000 PLM training run (~15x cheaper); authors recommend PLMs under privacy/limited hardware | p. 42 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | GPT-4o ITFSP per-language function Acc: Go 0.8082 (best) to Python 0.6626 (worst); CodeT5P beats it in JavaScript (0.7062 vs 0.6642) | p. 21 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | Line-level F1 by language: JavaScript 0.7815 best, C# 0.4348 worst (CodeT5P better in C#, n = 13) | p. 8, p. 26 | V | weak |
| RQ4 | Memory-safety CWEs are hardest to localise: line-level correct rate CWE-787 6.25%, CWE-119 21.74%, CWE-125 27.27% (best model) | p. 30 | V | weak |
| RQ4 | LLM-only correct functions are more complex/longer (median CC 4.0 vs 2.0; 135.5 vs 96 tokens) than PLM-only correct ones; PLM handles deeper nesting | p. 34 | V | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "GPT-4o with instruction tuning and few-shot prompting demonstrates superior performance, achieving the highest accuracy (0.7196) at function-level compared to the best-performing CodeT5P (0.6037)" (p. 4)

> "the PLM remains superior in overall classification balance for this imbalanced dataset." (p. 41)

> "the size of LLMs is not the decisive factor affecting performance on multilingual vulnerability detection, and the use of reasoning LLMs does not lead to significant improvements." (p. 4)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: pp. 1-48 read in full (all sections, tables 1-12, threats, conclusion, declarations). The reference list (pp. 48-53) was skimmed. Figures 4, 5 and 8-10 are bar charts garbled by text extraction; we rely on the numbers the authors give in the text for them (p. 21, p. 26, p. 32, p. 34).
- Version: metadata = EMSE 2026 (DOI 10.1007/s10664-026-10832-4). The analysed text is arXiv 2506.07503v2 (10 Mar 2026), identity matched by arXiv id. The typeset journal version may differ slightly. The running header reads "W. Dong et al.", a template artifact.
- Uncertainties: (1) The padding hypothesis and the twin/BM25 leakage hypothesis (§9) are our inference from reported numbers; the replication package could settle both. (2) How GPT-3.5/GPT-4o were instruction-tuned (OpenAI fine-tuning API vs. other) is not stated; we infer the API from the Table 12 training costs (p. 41). (3) "Break-even after 58 runs" (p. 42) could not be reproduced from the stated numbers (4,650 / (86.07 − 1.34) ≈ 55); this is minor.

> Version note: the text analysed is arXiv 2506.07503v2 (10 Mar 2026, 53 pages, journal "manuscript No." template) (p. 1), not the typeset EMSE version. Page refs are PDF pages of this preprint.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Evaluate how well pre-trained code language models (PLMs) and large language models (LLMs) detect vulnerabilities across seven programming languages, at both function level and line level. Prior work focused on C/C++ and function-level detection (p. 1, p. 3, p. 4).
- [A] Working hypothesis: LLMs with suitable learning strategies (instruction tuning, few-shot prompting) improve multilingual function- and line-level detection (p. 4).
- [A] The paper extends the authors' ISSTA'25 workshop paper (Yu et al. 2025b) with embedding models, few-shot prompting and instruction tuning, line-level detection, CWE/severity analyses, and model size/reasoning experiments (p. 5).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- RQ1: How effective are PLMs and LLMs at detecting multilingual vulnerabilities at function level? (p. 4)
- RQ2: ... at line level? (p. 4)
- RQ3: What are the strengths and weaknesses of PLMs and LLMs in multilingual detection? (p. 4)
- Discussion experiments: code-structure analysis, model size (70B), reasoning LLMs, time-split leakage check, imbalanced setting, deployment cost (p. 32-p. 43).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: controlled empirical comparison on a fixed random 8:1:1 split, stratified by language, of the REEF dataset (p. 7, p. 8).
- Approach / model / intervention:
  - PLMs (function level): CodeBERT, CodeT5, CodeT5P, UniXcoder and LineVul, fully fine-tuned with an MLP head on the [CLS] token. OpenAI Text-Embedding-Ada-002 / 3-Small / 3-Large are used as frozen encoders with a trained classifier head (p. 9, p. 16).
  - PLMs (line level): CodeBERT, UniXcoder, CodeT5, CodeT5P, with up to 113 lines x 31 tokens per function, GRU per line, per-line sigmoid, threshold 0.5. LineVul and the embedding models are excluded at line level (p. 22).
  - LLMs: DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B, Code Llama 7B, Llama 3 8B (HuggingFace), GPT-3.5-Turbo (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125), GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) (p. 10, p. 15). Strategies: zero-shot; few-shot with 3 BM25-retrieved training examples; instruction tuning (LoRA) followed by zero-shot or few-shot prompting (p. 12, p. 14). GRACE (AST-enhanced LLM, zero-shot) is added as a baseline at function level (p. 10, p. 11).
  - Line-level LLM prompts state that the function is vulnerable, and lines are tagged "Line N:" (p. 11, p. 23).
  - Extra models: Code Llama 70B and Llama 3 70B (p. 35); reasoning LLMs DeepSeek-R1 (671B) and QwQ-plus, zero-shot only (p. 37).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: dummy classifiers that predict all-vulnerable or all-clean (p. 11). **No static-analysis (SAST) tool and no GNN/RNN detector is evaluated.** GNNs/RNNs are excluded because ASTs are language-specific and PLMs were previously shown to be better (p. 9, p. 10). MSIVD and Vul-RAG are excluded for lack of multilingual knowledge/explanations (p. 11).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): REEF (Wang et al. 2023a): 4,466 CVEs, 30,987 patches, NVD + Mend CVE list, 2016-2023, seven languages (p. 6).
- Sampling / selection method: comments removed; functions extracted with Tree-sitter; the pre-change function is labelled vulnerable and the post-change function clean (matched by name, then by edit distance); functions longer than 512 removed (PLM input limit) (p. 6). Line labels come from deleted lines (difflib); vulnerable functions fixed by additions only are dropped (p. 6, p. 7). Split: 8:1:1 stratified random sampling per language (p. 7, p. 8). "Exact-match filtering" against leakage (p. 44).
- Sample size (N) and unit:
  - Function level: 20,165 functions (10,133 vulnerable / 10,032 clean); train 16,126 / val 2,013 / test 2,026. Per language: C 3,056; C++ 1,792; C# 427; Go 2,905; Java 3,235; JavaScript 5,468; Python 3,282. Test sets per language: C 307, C++ 181, C# 44, Go 292, Java 325, JavaScript 548, Python 329 (p. 7, Table 1).
  - Line level: 8,134 vulnerable functions (train 6,513 / val 811 / test 810); 25,161 vulnerable vs 150,607 non-vulnerable lines. C# test set has only 13 functions (p. 8, Table 2).
  - Tree-sitter extraction check: 377 random samples, 93% / 92% judged correct by two authors, Cohen's kappa 0.9448 (p. 7).
  - Severity: 1.2% low, 41.12% high, 25.09% critical (CVSS v4.0) (p. 8).
  - Time-split set (2024-2025, same pipeline): 3,138 function-level samples (balanced) and 1,328 line-level samples (p. 38).
  - Imbalanced set (benign functions mined from unchanged functions): train 48,219 / val 6,012 / test 6,051; test = 1,019 vulnerable + 5,032 benign (p. 39).
- Data availability (public? link?): data, training and evaluation scripts on GitHub (SpanShu96/Large-Language-Model-for-Multilingual-Vulnerability-Detection) (p. 48).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: PLMs replicated following Steenhoek et al. 2024a, using the original authors' hyper-parameters (p. 15, p. 43). LoRA for instruction tuning (p. 14, p. 16). Hardware: Xeon Gold 6342, 512 GB RAM, 2 x A800 GPUs (p. 16). Detailed hyper-parameters (learning rate, epochs, LoRA rank, temperature/decoding) are not reported in the paper; it refers to the replication package (p. 16). How GPT-3.5/GPT-4o were instruction-tuned is not described explicitly, but Table 12 lists per-token training costs for them (p. 41).
- Metrics are pooled over all test samples across languages, not averaged per language (p. 15).
- Code availability: yes (p. 48).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (binary), FPR, FNR, MCC, AUC (trapezoidal) (p. 14, p. 15). Accuracy is the primary metric at function level because the data is balanced; F1 is primary at line level because the data is imbalanced (p. 17, p. 23). RQ3 uses the share of correct detections per Top-25 CWE (2023 list) and per CVSS severity, plus Venn diagrams of unique correct/incorrect predictions (p. 27, p. 28).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): **none.** No significance tests, confidence intervals or repeated runs/seeds are reported. The words "significantly" and "significant" are used without tests (e.g. p. 21, p. 26, p. 38).

## 7. Key findings
1. Function level, balanced (Table 3): best LLM = GPT-4o with instruction tuning + few-shot (ITFSP): Acc 0.7196, P 0.7454, R 0.6722, F1 0.7069, FPR 0.2324, MCC 0.4360, AUC 0.7169. Best PLM = CodeT5P: Acc 0.6037, P 0.5626, R 0.9529, F1 0.7075, FPR 0.7496, MCC 0.2860, AUC 0.6015 — [V] (p. 17). F1 is essentially tied (0.7069 vs 0.7075); the gap is in accuracy/precision/FPR/MCC.
2. Every other LLM configuration at function level is near chance: zero-shot accuracy 0.4827-0.5061 (GRACE 0.5061), MCC −0.0585 to 0.0244; few-shot without tuning lowers accuracy for all but GPT-4o (e.g. GPT-3.5 0.3618, DeepSeek-Coder 0.3870); best instruction-tuned zero-shot is GPT-4o at 0.5874 — [V] (p. 17, p. 19).
3. Text-embedding models, CodeBERT and LineVul are near random at function level (Acc 0.5030-0.5173, AUC 0.50-0.51; LineVul and CodeBERT rows identical) — [V] (p. 17).
4. Per language, function level (Acc): GPT-4o ITFSP — C 0.7557, C# 0.7273, C++ 0.7901, Go 0.8082, JavaScript 0.6642, Java 0.7169, Python 0.6626. CodeT5P — C 0.5081, C# 0.6136, C++ 0.5249, Go 0.6062, JavaScript 0.7062, Java 0.6031, Python 0.5623 — [V] (p. 21). In JavaScript, CodeT5P (0.7062) and CodeT5 (0.6898) beat GPT-4o (0.6642). This contradicts the claim that GPT-4o "outperformed all other PLMs and LLMs across all seven studied languages" (p. 22) — [V] (p. 21, p. 22).
5. Line level (Table 4): GPT-4o ITFSP F1 0.6641 (P 0.7012, R 0.6307, MCC 0.6563, AUC 0.8116) vs best PLM CodeT5P F1 0.4841 (P 0.3536, R 0.7673, MCC 0.5029, AUC 0.8644). GPT-4o few-shot without tuning already gives F1 0.6050. Zero-shot LLM F1 is 0.2254-0.3313 — [V] (p. 23, p. 25, p. 26). CodeT5P has the higher AUC — [V] (p. 26).
6. Per language, line level (F1): GPT-4o ITFSP — C 0.5478, C# 0.4348, C++ 0.5774, Go 0.7078, JavaScript 0.7815, Java 0.6391, Python 0.6055. CodeT5P — C 0.3727, C# 0.4750, C++ 0.4768, Go 0.4146, JavaScript 0.6556, Java 0.4167, Python 0.4519 — [V] (p. 26). CodeT5P wins in C# (13 test functions) — [V] (p. 8, p. 26).
7. Imbalanced function-level setting (~17% vulnerable; Table 11): the ranking reverses. Best F1 is UniXcoder 0.4626 (MCC 0.3495); CodeT5P has the highest MCC 0.3627; GPT-4o ITFSP reaches F1 0.4010, MCC 0.2774. The authors conclude the PLM "remains superior in overall classification balance" in the imbalanced setting — [V] (p. 40, p. 41). Instruction-tuned GPT-4o zero-shot has P 0.9659 but R 0.0834 — [V] (p. 40).
8. Top-25 CWEs (function level, per-CWE accuracy over vulnerable + clean functions, 1,119 test items): GPT-4o ITFSP 75.87% vs CodeT5P 61.13%. It is best on 23 of 25 CWEs (CodeT5P leads or ties on 7); e.g. CWE-787 82.93% vs 56.1%, CWE-79 78.28% vs 63.13%, CWE-89 78.26% vs 58.7% — [V] (p. 29, p. 30, Table 5).
9. Top-25 CWEs (line level, 441 items): GPT-4o ITFSP 50.79% vs CodeT5P 21.77%. Memory-safety CWEs are hardest: CWE-787 1/16 (6.25%), CWE-119 21.74%, CWE-125 27.27% — [V] (p. 30, Table 6). The authors find 11 CWEs, including CWE-787, CWE-125 and CWE-22, are "detected" at function level but not at line level — [A] (p. 31).
10. Severity: at function level GPT-4o ITFSP has 630 correct High-severity detections vs CodeT5P 514, but fewer Critical (305 vs 321). At line level, 134 Critical vs 76 — [V] (p. 32).
11. Complementarity: CodeT5P has the most unique correct function-level detections (108 vs 28 for GPT-4o ITFSP), but GPT-4o ITFSP has the fewest unique incorrect detections (11 vs 136) — [V] (p. 29). In 608 LLM-only-correct vs 370 PLM-only-correct functions, the LLM-only set has higher median cyclomatic complexity (4.0 vs 2.0), tokens (135.5 vs 96.0) and LOC (19 vs 15), but lower nesting (2.0 vs 3.0) — [V] (p. 32, p. 34).
12. Model size: 70B Code Llama / Llama 3 bring no function-level gain (accuracies 0.4659-0.5093). At line level, Llama 3 70B few-shot F1 is 0.5214 vs 0.2822 for 8B, while Code Llama 70B gets worse (0.2267 vs 0.3257) — [V] (p. 35, p. 36).
13. Reasoning LLMs (zero-shot): DeepSeek-R1 Acc 0.5217 / line F1 0.2746; QwQ-plus Acc 0.5346 / line F1 0.3136. Only slightly above random, and not better than non-reasoning LLMs at line level — [V] (p. 37, p. 38).
14. Time-split check (2024-2025 CVEs): GPT-4o ITFSP function-level Acc 0.7874, F1 0.7804, MCC 0.5767; line-level F1 0.3450, MCC 0.3301 (down from 0.6641 in-distribution) — [V] (p. 38, p. 39, Table 10). The authors conclude the LLM "does not merely memorize" — [A] (p. 39).
15. Cost: GPT-4o instruction tuning $86.07 (function) / $59.42 (line); inference input ≈$1.65 / $0.95 for the test set. A local A6000 PLM training run costs ≈$5.59 (≈15x cheaper), with break-even after 58 fine-tuning runs — [V] (p. 41, p. 42). The authors recommend PLMs for organisations with privacy constraints or only consumer GPUs — [A] (p. 42, p. 43).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Only the REEF dataset and seven languages; generalisation to other languages is unknown (p. 43).
- [A] The 512-token limit of the PLMs restricts context for longer code (p. 43).
- [A] Single-language specialised LLM detectors (mostly C/C++) are excluded, which limits comparison with customised tools (p. 43).
- [A] Tree-sitter may misidentify functions (sanity check done) (p. 43).
- [A] Leakage from the same project/developer across splits is possible; only exact-match filtering is applied (p. 44).
- [A] Tangled commits add label noise; heuristics reduce it, but line-level manual verification is future work (p. 44).
- [A] Reasoning LLMs were not fine-tuned with RL (p. 38).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **No static-analysis tool is compared.** For our RQ1, this paper supports only LLM-vs-DL/PLM claims, not LLM-vs-SAST. Based on §3 (p. 9-p. 11).
- [I] **The headline result rests on one configuration.** GPT-4o ITFSP is the only LLM setting clearly above chance at function level (next best 0.5874). Few-shot hurts every other model, and the paper gives no explanation, ablation, seed variation or test. A single strong outlier without variance estimates is fragile. Based on Table 3 (p. 17).
- [I] **Possible leakage via paired functions and BM25 retrieval.** The split is random at function level (p. 7), and each vulnerable function has its fixed twin labelled clean (p. 6). Twins and functions from the same CVE/project can fall on opposite sides of the split, and BM25 few-shot retrieval from the training set could then return a near-identical twin with the opposite label. Only exact-match filtering is applied (p. 44). This could favour the few-shot + fine-tuned setting. It is a hypothesis only; the paper gives no retrieval-overlap statistics. The time-split check (p. 38) tests memorisation of pre-training data, not this split-level overlap.
- [I] **Line-level accuracy/FPR are probably inflated by padding.** The DummyClf_vul precision on the line-level test set is 0.0267 (p. 23), i.e. 2.67% vulnerable lines. But Table 2 implies about 14.3% vulnerable lines (25,161 / 175,768) (p. 8). 810 test functions x 113 padded line slots ≈ 91,530 slots, and 2.67% of that ≈ 2,440 vulnerable lines, close to the ≈2,500 expected from the dataset average (3.1 per function). This suggests metrics are computed over padded 113-line slots. If so, accuracy (≈0.95-0.98) and FPR are inflated and not comparable to other papers. F1/precision/recall are less affected. Our arithmetic, unconfirmed by the authors.
- [I] The line-level task is easier than real use: only known-vulnerable functions are given, the LLM prompt says the function is vulnerable (p. 11), and only functions with deleted lines are kept (p. 7).
- [I] Short functions only: functions over 512 tokens are removed (p. 6), and median LOC in the divergent samples is 9-36 (p. 33). Scale effects (RQ4) are not tested.
- [I] The 2024-2025 time-split accuracy (0.7874) is higher than in-distribution (0.7196) (p. 39, p. 17). This is unusual and unexplained. Line-level F1 halves (0.6641 → 0.3450), which suggests that localisation does not generalise well over time (p. 39).
- [I] Text vs. table mismatches: CodeBERT Acc 0.5163 in the text vs 0.5173 in the table (p. 18 vs p. 17); GPT-3.5 zero-shot 0.4758 vs 0.4827 (p. 19 vs p. 17); UniXcoder MCC 0.3475 vs 0.3495 (p. 41 vs p. 40); GPT-4o imbalanced zero-shot F1 "0.1264" in the text vs 0.2036 in the table (p. 40). The model is called "GPT-4" in places (p. 21, p. 38). Minor issues, but signs of limited proofreading.
- [I] The per-CWE "correct detection" percentage mixes vulnerable and clean items. At line level, what counts as "correct" for a function is not defined (p. 29, p. 30).
- [I] Pooled metrics are dominated by JavaScript (548 of 2,026 function-level test items) (p. 7, p. 15). C# results rest on 44 / 13 test functions (p. 7, p. 8).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): random function-level split, not split by CVE, project or time (p. 7); possible twin/BM25 leakage (§9); possible padding effect on line-level metrics (§9); PLMs are reproduced from original hyper-parameters, while LLM prompt templates differ across strategies (p. 11, p. 13, p. 43).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): REEF only; seven languages; short functions (≤512 tokens) (p. 6, p. 43); balanced test (50/50) by default (p. 7). The imbalanced variant (p. 39) changes the conclusion.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): the line-level task presupposes a known-vulnerable function (p. 11). Labels come from fix commits (pre-change = vulnerable, post-change = clean) with known tangling noise (p. 6, p. 44). The authors report that two raters judged 92-93% of 377 extracted functions correct (p. 7).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no tests, confidence intervals or seeds. Many configurations (≈30) are compared on one split, and the best is chosen post hoc. Per-language and per-CWE cells are small (e.g. C# 44/13; CWE-862 n = 1) (p. 7, p. 8, p. 30).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): data and scripts are released (p. 48), and model versions are given for the OpenAI models (p. 15). Hyper-parameters, decoding settings and GPT fine-tuning details are not in the paper (p. 16).
- Funding: Chinese and Japanese public grants; no conflict of interest declared (p. 48).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: larger multilingual benchmarks; intermediate representations that unify code across languages; better PLM/LLM learning strategies such as multi-task learning or meta-learning to close the gap between high- and low-resource languages (p. 47); RL fine-tuning of reasoning LLMs (p. 38); line-level manual verification of labels (p. 44); adding specialised models as they support more languages (p. 43).
- Suggested by us [I]: add SAST baselines (CodeQL/Semgrep) on the same multilingual test split; split by CVE/project/time; repeat the GPT-4o ITFSP run with several seeds and BM25-overlap controls; compute line-level metrics on real lines only; evaluate realistic class ratios as the main setting.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (LLM vs DL/PLM head-to-head; no SAST), RQ2 (balanced vs imbalanced reversal; time split; pooled metrics; line-level setup), RQ3 (cost/TCO of API LLM vs local PLM; no hybrid), RQ4 (per-language, per-CWE, per-severity, function complexity), RQ5 (leakage, granularity, imbalance).
- How it informs our work [I]: one of the few multilingual, two-granularity LLM-vs-PLM comparisons. Its main lesson for the review is conditional: only a fine-tuned frontier LLM with retrieved examples beats fine-tuned PLMs, and only on balanced data. Under realistic imbalance, fine-tuned PLMs match or beat it. Prompt-only LLMs are near chance at function level. This supports a "results depend on setup" answer to RQ2.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | On balanced REEF (7 languages), fine-tuned GPT-4o + BM25 few-shot beats best PLM CodeT5P at function level (Acc 0.7196 vs 0.6037; MCC 0.4360 vs 0.2860; F1 tied 0.7069 vs 0.7075) | p. 17 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | Prompt-only LLMs (zero-/few-shot, incl. GPT-4o, GRACE, DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-plus) are near chance at function level (Acc 0.36-0.53, MCC ≤0.07) | p. 17, p. 37 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | Line level: GPT-4o ITFSP F1 0.6641 vs CodeT5P 0.4841 (but CodeT5P AUC 0.8644 > 0.8116) | p. 23, p. 26 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Under realistic imbalance (~17% vulnerable), PLMs outperform the best LLM (UniXcoder F1 0.4626 / CodeT5P MCC 0.3627 vs GPT-4o ITFSP F1 0.4010 / MCC 0.2774) — conclusion flips with class ratio | p. 40, p. 41 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Time-split (2024-2025) GPT-4o ITFSP keeps function-level Acc 0.7874 but line-level F1 drops to 0.3450 from 0.6641 | p. 39 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Random function-level split with paired vulnerable/fixed twins and BM25 few-shot retrieval from train; only exact-match dedup — possible leakage favouring ITFSP | p. 6, p. 7, p. 44 | I | weak |
| RQ2 | Line-level dummy precision 0.0267 vs ~14% vulnerable lines in dataset suggests metrics over padded 113-line slots, inflating accuracy/FPR | p. 8, p. 22, p. 23 | I | weak |
| RQ3 | GPT-4o instruction tuning costs $86.07 (function) vs ≈$5.59 per local A6000 PLM training run (~15x cheaper); authors recommend PLMs under privacy/limited hardware | p. 42 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | GPT-4o ITFSP per-language function Acc: Go 0.8082 (best) to Python 0.6626 (worst); CodeT5P beats it in JavaScript (0.7062 vs 0.6642) | p. 21 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | Line-level F1 by language: JavaScript 0.7815 best, C# 0.4348 worst (CodeT5P better in C#, n = 13) | p. 8, p. 26 | V | weak |
| RQ4 | Memory-safety CWEs are hardest to localise: line-level correct rate CWE-787 6.25%, CWE-119 21.74%, CWE-125 27.27% (best model) | p. 30 | V | weak |
| RQ4 | LLM-only correct functions are more complex/longer (median CC 4.0 vs 2.0; 135.5 vs 96 tokens) than PLM-only correct ones; PLM handles deeper nesting | p. 34 | V | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "GPT-4o with instruction tuning and few-shot prompting demonstrates superior performance, achieving the highest accuracy (0.7196) at function-level compared to the best-performing CodeT5P (0.6037)" (p. 4)

> "the PLM remains superior in overall classification balance for this imbalanced dataset." (p. 41)

> "the size of LLMs is not the decisive factor affecting performance on multilingual vulnerability detection, and the use of reasoning LLMs does not lead to significant improvements." (p. 4)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: pp. 1-48 read in full (all sections, tables 1-12, threats, conclusion, declarations). The reference list (pp. 48-53) was skimmed. Figures 4, 5 and 8-10 are bar charts garbled by text extraction; we rely on the numbers the authors give in the text for them (p. 21, p. 26, p. 32, p. 34).
- Version: metadata = EMSE 2026 (DOI 10.1007/s10664-026-10832-4). The analysed text is arXiv 2506.07503v2 (10 Mar 2026), identity matched by arXiv id. The typeset journal version may differ slightly. The running header reads "W. Dong et al.", a template artifact.
- Uncertainties: (1) The padding hypothesis and the twin/BM25 leakage hypothesis (§9) are our inference from reported numbers; the replication package could settle both. (2) How GPT-3.5/GPT-4o were instruction-tuned (OpenAI fine-tuning API vs. other) is not stated; we infer the API from the Table 12 training costs (p. 41). (3) "Break-even after 58 runs" (p. 42) could not be reproduced from the stated numbers (4,650 / (86.07 − 1.34) ≈ 55); this is minor.

## ahmed2026secvuleval · ready · full-text (preprint)
**Version:** the text is arXiv 2505.19828v1, "SecVulEval: Benchmarking LLMs for Real-World C/C++ Vulnerability Detection", marked "Preprint. Under review". PDF p. 1 shows the same five York University authors, so it is the right paper; only the title changed. Analyst notes say the analysis is based on the preprint and Table 3 should be re-checked against the published AIware 2026 version.

**Summary:** A de-duplicated C/C++ benchmark: 25,440 functions, 5,867 CVEs, 145 CWEs, with statement-level labels and context labels generated by GPT-4.1. Five LLMs run in a 5-agent pipeline on 300 manually judged functions. The best, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, reaches 23.83% statement-level F1 and 53.89% function-level F1. There are no SAST, deep-learning or single-prompt baselines.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1 [V] p. 8, moderate: statement-level F1 is 23.83% (Claude), 22.38% (GPT-4.1), 15.31% (Codestral), 13.57% (Qwen), 7.14% (Deepseek). Function-level F1 is 35.20–53.89% and function-level precision is at most 47.41%.
- RQ2 [V] p. 8, moderate: requiring the correct statements plus correct reasoning more than halves F1 (GPT-4.1: 52.25% → 22.38%).
- RQ2 [V] p. 3, p. 6, moderate: the dataset has 0% duplicates; earlier datasets have up to 18.9%.
- RQ2 [I] p. 7, p. 8, p. 13, moderate: the statement-level recall seems to be computed differently from the paper's own definition (see below).
- RQ4 [V] p. 13, moderate: detected functions have a median of 14–33 lines of code, missed ones 64–71 (Mann-Whitney p ≤ 0.0168 for all five models).
- RQ4 [A] p. 13, weak: GPT-4.1 and Claude over-flag CWE-476, CWE-416 and CWE-190. They flagged 214–215 of 300 functions as vulnerable when 120 were.
- RQ5 [V] p. 9, moderate: models identify the needed context poorly (at most 41.33% per context type; function arguments at most 5.31%; environment context 0%).
- RQ3 [V] p. 17, moderate: open 22–33B models take about 5–8 minutes per function on 4 × L40S GPUs.

**Surprising or doubtful:**
- **Recall inflation.** I rebuilt whole-number counts from Table 3 and the flag counts on p. 13 (Claude: 215 flagged, 90 correct at function level, 119 vulnerable, 33 correct at statement level). Every reported statement-level recall comes out exactly as statement-level hits ÷ (statement-level hits + functions missed entirely). So "right function, wrong reasoning" cases were not counted as misses, although p. 7 says they should be. Under the paper's own definition, Claude's recall would be about 27.7% (not 53.23%) and F1 about 19.8% (not 23.83%). GPT-4.1's recall would be about 26.1% (not 49.21%). This is my inference, labelled [I].
- The implied number of vulnerable functions differs by model (119–126), although the paper says 120.
- The context "ground truth" was generated by GPT-4.1, which is also one of the models evaluated on it.
- 300 samples, a single run, and no confidence intervals.

**Incomplete sections:** none.

## shu2026evaluating · ready · full-text
**Version:** the text is arXiv 2506.07503v2 (10 Mar 2026, 53 pages), recorded in the file.

**Summary:** Eight pre-trained code models or embedding encoders (CodeBERT, CodeT5/CodeT5P, UniXcoder, LineVul, 3 OpenAI embedding encoders) are compared with five LLMs (zero-shot, few-shot with 3 retrieved examples, instruction tuning) on REEF across seven languages, at function and line level. On balanced data, fine-tuned GPT-4o with retrieved few-shot examples (GPT-4o ITFSP) beats CodeT5P (accuracy 0.7196 vs 0.6037; line-level F1 0.6641 vs 0.4841). On the imbalanced set (~17% vulnerable) the pre-trained models win. There are no SAST or graph-network baselines.

**Per-language numbers:**
- Function-level accuracy, GPT-4o ITFSP / CodeT5P: C 0.7557/0.5081, C# 0.7273/0.6136, C++ 0.7901/0.5249, Go 0.8082/0.6062, JavaScript 0.6642/0.7062, Java 0.7169/0.6031, Python 0.6626/0.5623 (p. 21).
- Line-level F1, GPT-4o ITFSP / CodeT5P: C 0.5478/0.3727, C# 0.4348/0.4750, C++ 0.5774/0.4768, Go 0.7078/0.4146, JavaScript 0.7815/0.6556, Java 0.6391/0.4167, Python 0.6055/0.4519 (p. 26).

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1 [V] p. 17, moderate: on balanced data GPT-4o ITFSP beats CodeT5P (accuracy 0.7196 vs 0.6037; MCC 0.4360 vs 0.2860), but F1 is tied (0.7069 vs 0.7075).
- RQ1 [V] p. 17, p. 37, moderate: prompt-only LLMs, including GPT-4o, GRACE, DeepSeek-R1 and QwQ-plus, are near chance (accuracy 0.36–0.53, MCC ≤ 0.07).
- RQ1 [V] p. 23, p. 26, moderate: line-level F1 is 0.6641 vs 0.4841, but CodeT5P has the higher AUC (0.8644 vs 0.8116).
- RQ2 [V] p. 40–41, moderate: on the imbalanced set the ranking flips. UniXcoder gets F1 0.4626 and CodeT5P MCC 0.3627, vs GPT-4o ITFSP at 0.4010 and 0.2774.
- RQ2 [V] p. 39, moderate: on 2024–2025 CVEs, function-level accuracy is 0.7874 but line-level F1 drops from 0.6641 to 0.3450.
- RQ2 [I], weak: possible split leakage and inflated line-level metrics (see below).
- RQ3 [V] p. 42, moderate: GPT-4o tuning costs $86.07 vs about $5.59 per local A6000 training run (~15x cheaper).
- RQ4 [V] p. 21, p. 26, moderate/weak: best function-level language is Go and worst is Python; line-level F1 is best in JavaScript (0.7815) and worst in C# (0.4348, only 13 test functions).
- RQ4 [V] p. 30, weak: memory-safety CWEs are hardest to localise (CWE-787 6.25%, CWE-119 21.74%, CWE-125 27.27%).
- RQ4 [V] p. 34, weak: functions only the LLM gets right are more complex and longer than those only the pre-trained model gets right; the pre-trained model does better on deeper nesting.

**Surprising or doubtful:**
- The paper says GPT-4o ITFSP beats all models "across all seven languages" (function level, p. 22). Its own p. 21 numbers contradict this for JavaScript: CodeT5P 0.7062 and CodeT5 0.6898 vs GPT-4o 0.6642.
- The result rests on one configuration. GPT-4o ITFSP is the only LLM setting clearly above chance (the next best is 0.5874), and few-shot makes every other model worse. There are no seeds or tests, though "significantly" is used throughout.
- **Possible leakage [I]:** the split is random at function level, each vulnerable function's fixed twin is in the data labelled clean, and few-shot examples are retrieved from the training set. Only exact-match filtering is applied, so a near-identical twin can sit on the other side of the split.
- **Line-level metrics [I]:** the always-vulnerable baseline has precision 0.0267, but the dataset has about 14.3% vulnerable lines. That fits metrics computed over 113 padded line slots per function, which would inflate accuracy and false-positive rate.
- Accuracy on the 2024–2025 split (0.7874) is higher than on the original test set (0.7196), which is unexplained.
- Several numbers in the text differ from the tables (CodeBERT accuracy, GPT-3.5 zero-shot, UniXcoder MCC, imbalanced GPT-4o F1), and the model is called "GPT-4" in places. Training details and how GPT-4o was fine-tuned are not reported.

**Incomplete sections:** none. Several figures are bar charts that did not extract as text, so per-language values for models other than GPT-4o and CodeT5P are not available.
